speakeroldname: Hon. E. J. Benson (Minister of Finance):
subtopic: FINANCE
subsubtopic: EFFECT ON CANADA. OF INCREASE IN U.S. PRIME LENDING RATE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the increase in the prime lending rates charged by United States banks has spread rapidly from New York, where it began, to other major United States cities. We must expect that all borrowers from United States banks will be affected, including international corporations with operations in Canada, and those Canadian companies which traditionally have looked to United States banks for part of their credit needs.
Some of the demand for credit from these borrowers will undoubtedly be reflected to Canadian banks. I am sure the Canadian banks will regard the needs of their regular Canadian customers as having first priority, but it is inevitable that some of the pressure on Canadian banks for loans will have to be dealt with by an increase in lending rates of the banks.

subtopic: FINANCE
subsubtopic: EFFECT ON CANADA. OF INCREASE IN U.S. PRIME LENDING RATE
speechtext: I take it from what the minister has said that he proposes to take no measures in this regard. Would he say whether the anticipated increase in bank rates in Canada might spread throughout our whole interest rates structure? Can he tell us, also, whether he has had an opportunity to confer with his officials, and whether he anticipates that this development will have any effect upon holdings of Canadian savings bonds?

subtopic: FINANCE
subsubtopic: EFFECT ON CANADA. OF INCREASE IN U.S. PRIME LENDING RATE
speechtext: I do not really think that at this point it will have a serious effect on holdings of Canadian savings bonds. However, we in Canada must always be mindful of the need to protect the position of our foreign exchange reserves. Since we have a free economy permitting loans to be made back and forth across the border it is inevitable that our bank rates must be somewhat aligned with those in the United States. However, at present I do not anticipate any difficulty with regard to Canadian savings bonds.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in spite of the numerous interjections last night by the Postmaster General (Mr. Kierans) and the Minister of Finance
DEBATES	9933
The Budget-Mr. Thompson (Mr. Benson) I will still limit my remarks to a few minutes.
The Minister of Finance asked me last night to define the gross national product. Frankly, I am amazed that a man in his position is not well enough informed to know this rudimentary fact. For his information, and I would hope his edification, may I say that the gross national product, by totalling all costs arising in production, measures the market value of all final goods and services produced in the current period by Canadian factors of production. It is equal to national income plus net indirect taxes, indirect taxes less subsidies, plus capital consumption allowances and miscellaneous valuation of adjustments.
This is something far different from the net income of the nation and its citizens which at factor cost measures the current earnings of Canadian factors of production, that is, land, labour and capital, from productive activity. It includes wages and salaries, profits, interest, net rent and net income of farm and non-farm unincorporated business.
According to page 79 of the budget papers presented to parliament by the Minister of Finance just prior to the budget, the gross national product of Canada in 1968 was $63,368 billion. The net national income for Canada in 1968 was $50,628 billion. On page 125 of the white paper it is stated that the federal budgetary expenditure was $12,058 billion. The combined provincial and municipal governmental expenditure for 1968 was something over $13 billion. On page 41 of the budget papers it is stated that the total government revenues for 1968, that is, federal, provincial and municipal revenues, exclusive of all intergovernmental transfers and not including borrowings or deficit spendings, amounted to $24.2 billion.
This figure of $24.2 billion represents the net total of taxes collected by governments at all levels during 1968. With the total amount of the actual income of all Canadians amounting in 1968 to $50,628 billion, the percentage of income taken from the Canadian taxpayers' pockets by the various tax collectors amounts to just over 47 per cent. I stated last night that it was nearly 50 per cent. As I did not have the actual statistics for 1968 before me, I could not give the specific percentage at that time, which we now find has passed 47 per cent for the first time.
My concern is twofold. First, the percentage of the income of Canadians required by the government has reached dangerously high
June 10, 1969

The Budget-Mr. Weatherhead levels. Historically, no free society has survived when the amount of its citizens' income required by government has passed 50 per cent. We are moving continually and continuously nearer that mark. The budget of the Minister of Finance does nothing to reverse this trend. Under his direction, thus far at least, the country is moving relentlessly toward an economic crisis.
Second, the urgent needs of municipal governments are rapidly bringing that level of government to a crisis of vast proportions. The need of new tax resources and capital financing just to provide the basic public needs for schools, hospitals, housing and essential services is great, far beyond the present reaches of that vital level of government. This budget does not do anything to alleviate the situation but rather aggravates the looming financial crisis.
In closing my remarks may I say it is one thing to gloat smugly over a balanced budget and quite another to provide a viable alternative which offers some hope for the future. The general consensus of government economists is that higher taxes, higher interest rates and tight money will eventually stop inflation. It may slow it down for the moment, but if these methods would ultimately accomplish that objective it would have been reached long ago.
What this country needs is an adequate financial policy which represents major surgery. The aspirin treatment provided now and perpetuated by the Minister of Finance from his Liberal predecessors is not good enough. I hope that in his promised white paper on the financial and fiscal situation in the nation he will deal with root causes, not just symptoms. The economy of this country will not survive simply on more and more palliatives. I suggest that the Minister of Finance come down out of the clouds and face the reality of the situation before a financial crisis breaks upon us.

subtopic: THE BUDGET
subsubtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first of all I would like to congratulate the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) for bringing down a budget last week which is aimed directly at two of the main problems facing Canada at this time, namely, inflation or the ever-increasing cost of living, and regional economic disparity. The fact that he has been able to do so without increasing the rate of income tax, sales tax, corporation tax or excise tax, while at the same time anticipating the first balanced

budget in 13 years with a surplus of about $250 million, is very commendable.
There are, of course, other problems affecting the country, including those between the French and English linguistic groups and the serious urban problems of housing, pollution, transportation, etc,, of which those of us from the cities of Canada are very much aware. I would like to refer to them again later in my remarks.
The budget forecasts the continued general prosperity of Canada in recent years, and notes a general decline in unemployment during the last 12 months, as well as a real increase of the gross national product of over 5 per cent which is expected for this fiscal year. While everything possible should be done to decrease inflation and decrease unemployment, which are not always compatible, Canada as a world trading nation is directly affected by the general economic and fiscal conditions of the world because of our close economic ties, especially with financial and economic conditions in the United States. The extremely heavy cost of the war in Viet Nam for the United States has resulted in financial difficulties and inflationary pressures which reverberate into Canada. An end to that war would probably decrease inflation in Canada more than any other single factor, but we have little control over that.
There are many ways in which the government can fight inflation, and apart from the measures in this budget there has been considerable recent government action in this regard. The prices and incomes commission recently set up by the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Basford) will be a valuable new element in Canada's battle against inflation. It will inquire into and report upon the causes, processes and consequences of inflation, and will inform the government and the general public how price stability can best be achieved. If this Commission and the other government measures are not as successful as hoped for in this regard, I believe serious thought will have to be given to granting such a commission, or a similar one, more direct powers toward controlling spiralling prices and incomes, although I trust such a step will not prove necessary. In any event, inflation which steals from everyone, and particularly hits hard at the poorer, older people on modest fixed and semi-fixed incomes and pensions, will have to continue to be attacked by all levels of government, and this budget and recent federal government action go a long way in this regard.
June 10, 1969	COMMONS
The pegging of Department of National Defence expenditures at their figure of $1.8 billion which is now about 16 per cent of our expenditures, and the thorough review of other government spending programs with a view to cutting out unessentials, are further evidence that the federal government is serious about this matter. Our defence and foreign policies are still undergoing reviews, and while Canada will always want to play her full part in international affairs it may still be that we are not getting the best value for our $1.8 billion spent on national defence and that we could cut our expenditures somewhat in this field without jeopardizing our true effectiveness in the world.
The extension of the 3 per cent surtax for another year on income and corporation tax affects mainly those making over $10,000 to $12,000 a year and will continue for another year, primarily as an anti-inflationary measure.
The immediate implementation of the final tariff rates agreed to by Canada during the Kennedy Round negotiations should spur more vigorous price competition and efficiency of production in our Canadian plants. Freer trade has been a classic principle of Liberalism, and while it may cause short term problems in some industries and plants, reduced tariffs on $2.1 billion of imports of raw materials and finished goods will result in somewhat reduced prices to consumers in many items. The announcement by the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs that he will establish some machinery to ensure that savings by reason of these tariff reductions will be passed on to the consumer is also encouraging in this fight against inflation. That minister is to be congratulated for his zeal in continually thinking of ways to give the consumer a better break.
The other main anti-inflation measure in the budget, and one with regional development undertones, is the deferring of capital cost allowances for two years on commercial buildings put in place to the end of 1970 in cities of over 50,000 in Ontario, Alberta and British Columbia.
This, of course, affects metropolitan Toronto more than any other city, since our city has by far the largest number of commercial projects in the active planning stage of any city in Canada. It was on this basis that the Toronto Telegram in an editorial on June 5 stated that Toronto members of parliament should blast the new budget, which in its words discriminates against Toronto and
DEBATES	9935
The Budget-Mr. Weatherhead other Ontario cities. As a lifelong resident of metropolitan Toronto and as one who represents some 90,000 of its citizens in this parliament, I am very disappointed at the parochial, narrow and shortsighted attitude of that newspaper as represented in that editorial.

The government wishes to reduce pressure on the construction industry which is a trendsetter in the escalation of prices and costs in general, in the economy as a whole. In the construction industry new commercial buildings were scheduled to increase the most, and most of this increase was to be in the big cities of those three provinces. This meant that commercial building enterprises would be bidding in the market for scarce labour and scarce financing in competition with essential and badly needed housing and industrial building projects.
Accordingly, it is the purpose of this budget policy to hit at one cause of inflation at its source, the heavy investment in new commercial buildings in the big cities of the three provinces, while exempting the other provinces and all the smaller communities because of higher unemployment and slower economic growth in those areas. It recognizes the very important principle that inflation and other economic problems can be regional in nature.
While this is mainly an anti-inflation measure, its two-side effects are the desire that more and cheaper financing will be available for housing and industrial projects in these 22 cities affected, and that there will be an increase in commercial building in the slower development areas of our country.
I hope that this is the case, but I believe that if this part of the budget is to be criticized it is because it may not go far enough in putting a damper on commercial building in the high-growth cities for more effective anti-inflation results and for more beneficial increased housing and regional development aspects. The regulations will exempt structures for which firm commitments have been made. It appears also, at this very early date, that at least some of the other commercial buildings will not be deterred by the deferral of capital cost allowance of usually 5 per cent per year, because of the effect that, a 4 per cent, let us say, annual inflation in building costs would have, if the projects were delayed for two years. However, it still should make some more financing available to

The Budget-Mr. Weatherhead housing and industrial development in Toronto and the 21 other urban areas, and will probably help divert some additional commercial activity to more underdeveloped areas. It is because of the commendable aspects of this budget policy as anti-inflationary, an aid to housing financing, and as some aid to underdeveloped areas without hurting the booming economy of Metro Toronto to any real extent, that I took such exception to the comments of the said newspaper.
There are many important projects, Mr. Speaker, in or near Metropolitan Toronto at the present time in which the federal government is or should be directly involved-the whole housing area under the National Housing Act and Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, the waterfront development plan, the C.N.-C.P.R. downtown complex, the urban renewal areas, the considerable expansion of Malton airport and making it more international in character, the location and building of a second international airport, the C.N.E., a new downtown post office complex and new suburban stations, and its participation in flood control aspects of acquiring land for the Metropolitan Toronto and Region Conservation Authority. I and other Members of Parliament from Toronto have no hesitation in promoting these and other Toronto area matters with the federal government, and our Toronto area Liberal caucus has had numerous meetings with municipal and federal government officials during the last year on these and other matters with considerable success. However, this does not mean that we are blind to the needs of the rest of the country, particularly the more underdeveloped areas, and while promoting the legitimate federal concern in Toronto we will support wholeheartedly proposals such as just discussed in this budget which attack regional disparity.
Time will tell whether this budget policy with respect to commercial buildings is as effective as hoped, but the principle that policies to fight inflation need not and should not apply in the same way to all regions is an excellent one, and more stringent regulations can always be included in the budget next year if necessary.
About 80 per cent of the constituencies in these 22 cities, Mr. Speaker, are represented by Liberal Members of Parliament and we make up nearly 40 per cent of the total number of Liberal members. In the rest of the country we hold only 45 per cent of the seats and the opposition parties hold 55 per cent. I

think that this reiterates the government's determination to attack inflation and regional disparity despite the fact that the government party is so strong in the 22 urban areas that will feel the brunt of the deferred capital cost and lower tariff policies.
Along with the benefit the deferred capital cost policy will have in underdeveloped areas, with the regional development incentives bill recently introduced by the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion (Mr. Mar-chand) should play a very important role in overcoming disparities in economic and social development between regions in Canada. The granting of up to $12 million for each new manufacturing company which will contribute substantially to employment in designated slow-growth areas should prove a strong incentive to the establishment of badly needed plants in these more economically backward areas. This combined with heavy federal investment in the comprehensive redevelopment of Prince Edward Island announced earlier this year will go a long way toward making a more just society in these underdeveloped areas. This is so important not only for the people living there but for the whole country, since Canada will be unable to survive as a country unless the gulf between the affluent and poor areas of the country is narrowed as quickly as possible.
In passing, Mr. Speaker, perhaps I could be permitted to express my support for the languages bill now being considered by a committee of the house and which, I am sure, the house will pass within the next few days. As one born in Toronto of English-Irish ancestry, including United Empire Loyalist stock who came to Canada nearly 200 years ago, my support of the bill might be suspect to some people. However, I strongly believe that our two most numerous linguistic groups and the only main ones that were here at the time of confederation, should have the right to conduct business affairs in their own language in federal government departments across the country in areas where they make up a significant proportion of the population. Despite my Anglo-Saxon background I am lucky enough to be married to a girl of Ukrainian background and therefore appreciate a little the view of some of our Canadians whose native language is neither English nor French. I believe we have been extremely fortunate in the high quality of all our immigrants, but the English and French linguistic rights as official languages were established before confederation and I believe they
June 10, 1969	COMMONS
should remain so without in any way detracting from the worth or importance of the languages or cultures of all our excellent Canadians of a non-English or French linguistic background.
One of the pleasant by-products of being a Member of Parliament, Mr. Speaker, is the opportunity we get to learn English or French, if we wish to do so, under excellent instructors. I have been taking instruction in French since last October, with one of the groups of English-speaking M.P.s, four hours a week in Ottawa, with periodic immersion courses of one to two weeks at St. Jean, Quebec, and perhaps in next year's budget debate I will be able to perform partly in French.
I would like to say, Mr. Speaker, that my riding in the east end of Metropolitan Toronto is part of a traditionally strong Anglo-Saxon, Protestant area of the city. However, I campaigned last year on the need for bilingual districts and a bill such as the one above-mentioned, and I have received not one letter of complaint about this bill since it was introduced last fall. I wish I could say the same thing about some of our other policies and bills. I am sure that the people of Scarborough West and Metropolitan Toronto, in general, are quite agreeable to the implementation of the languages bill as an essential aid to national unity.
Since one of the reasons for the deferred capital cost allowances on commercial buildings was to divert more scarce capital and labour into new housing, perhaps I could close my comments, Mr. Speaker, with some remarks on this all-important subject, particularly for those of us who come from the Metropolitan Toronto area. I have been very interested in housing and urban policies, and in my maiden speech last fall referred to some of the proposals I and other elected officials from Scarborough made to the housing task force last October. I read the task force report with interest when it came out at the end of January, agreeing broadly with it, and then I was somewhat disturbed by the sudden resignation of the hon. member for Trinity (Mr. Hellyer) as Minister of Transport. However, the immediate announcement by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) of many amendments to the National Housing Act and regulations, and the additional details given by the new minister responsible for housing on second reading of the bill recently, exceeded my expectations and
DEBATES	9937
The Budget-Mr. Weatherhead should go a long way with Ontario government co-operation to help alleviate the housing problem in Metropolitan Toronto and in other areas of the country.
[DOT] (3:10 p.m.)
The fact that the federal government will now lend 90 per cent of the cost of acquiring land to either the province or municipality with provincial consent, for either public or private housing, should clear the way for substantial tracts of land or land banks being acquired in the outer suburban districts of Metro Toronto and the larger cities. This land, after servicing, will be sold as building lots for considerably less than the going rates, which should have the beneficial effect of decreasing land values in the whole area. To make it effective large tracts will have to be acquired around Metro, and the land is so expensive now that huge sums of money will be involved. However, the federal moneys are just loans and will be repaid, I suppose on a revolving fund basis.
The paying of a 50 per cent subsidy by the federal government on apartments and homes rented by Ontario Housing Corporation and similar agencies in other provinces will mean in Metropolitan Toronto that O.H.C. will be able to rent many more individual apartment units, which will go a long way toward satisfying the nearly 14,000 applicants waiting for same. The lifting of the freeze on public housing projects that have C.M.H.C. approval should also accommodate many more than those on the waiting list. However, I was happy to see the task force comments on the desirability of row type and more diversified public and private housing have not been forgotten, and that after consultations with the provinces new guidelines on this subject will be announced by early next year.
Increasing the maximum of National Housing Act mortgages to $25,000, extending the term to 40 years and cutting the mortgage insurance fee in half are very beneficial measures in my home area where new houses in our suburbs start at about $30,000. A $5,000 down payment will now suffice, rather than the $12,000 needed before when the N.H.A. maximum mortgage was $18,000.
Similarly, increasing N.H.A. mortgages to $18,000 on resale homes should make more mortgage money available for older homes and will allow O.H.C. tenants in many cases, with provincial approval, to buy on reasonable terms the homes in which they are now living.
June 10, 1969

The Budget-Mr. Weatherhead
The freeing of the interest rate and the reviewing of the rate every five years should make more mortgage money available at somewhat reduced rates. If it does not have that effect fairly quickly these proposals will have to be reviewed.
Increased federal loans to limited dividend housing and federal loans to buy up and renovate older homes in an urban development area, rather than having to level all the buildings to the ground, are among some of the other welcome amendments to this legislation.
There are, however, two policies in connection with housing that I believe are very important, which were favourably referred to in the task force report but which have yet to be implemented by the government. In my maiden speech I supported the creation of a separate government department of housing and urban development with its own cabinet minister, and 1 still think it is a good idea. The present minister responsible for housing is now a Minister without Portfolio, but without all the staff and facilities, independent of C.M.H.C., that a full minister of housing and urban affairs would have. The present minister is certainly to be congratulated on the speed at which he has moved since becoming the minister responsible for housing, and he would make an excellent first minister of a new department of housing and urban affairs.
Such a federal department would underline even further the federal government's interest and concern in those matters which affect about 75 per cent of all Canadians at the present time, those who live in our urban areas, without interfering in the constitutional jurisdiction of the provinces in this field. It could co-ordinate co-operation between the three levels of government with respect to urban matters, and also stress more greatly research into city problems at the government and university levels.
My second policy relates to the 11 per cent federal sales tax on building materials. I understand that this produces about $300 million in revenue for the federal government, which is no mean amount. However, if housing is not a national crisis, it surely is a very serious problem in metropolitan Toronto. The problem is not so much the lack of supply but the high price of the units available.

I wish to thank hon. members and I will be through in about two minutes.
The task force report found that the combined federal and provincial sales taxes can add up to $950 to the final price of a modest three bedroom bungalow. It appears to me somewhat incongruous that we and the provincial governments are keeping these sales taxes on residential building materials, while at the same time all our other governmental policies are aimed at driving the price of houses down. We have a surplus now of $250 million, and while I suppose every Member of Parliament has a favourite scheme for spending some or all of this surplus, I believe that if for inflation reasons we do not want to spend all of the surplus we could either cut the sales tax in stages annually, or perhaps could give rebates of tax on houses which cost, say, $20,000 or less, exclusive of land, as suggested by the task force. This would have a direct effect on reducing the price of new homes, which is what our legislation is trying to achieve.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Finance mentioned in his budget speech that the government white paper on tax reform will be coming out this summer. The legislation that comes out of this white paper will be among the most important of this 28th parliament, since it will substantially reform our present tax laws and make them far more fair and equitable for all.
With the rest of the country I am awaiting the government's proposals in this regard with great interest. In the meantime, despite my criticisms with respect to the sales tax, I would again like to congratulate the Minister of Finance on the general anti-inflation, regional development tenor of this budget.

speakeroldname: Hon. Robert L. Stanfield (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: THE BUDGET
subsubtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the first thing one must say about this budget or budgetary statement is that it proves the failure of the October budget presented by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson). This is clearly proved by the minister's own admission that inflation is not slowing down as he then predicted, making him not only a bad forecaster but a poor improviser or developer of policies. Actually, according to his own admission the rate of inflation this year will be at least as high as last year, when it was the highest it

June 10, 1969
had been for 17 years in Canada. Indeed, over the last 12 months, if I compare last May with May, 1968, the rate of increase in the cost of living index has been 4.7 per cent.
The minister says, of course, that things will be better in 1970, and that we should wait until then. We have been listening to this same old story since 1965 from successive Ministers of Finance across the way. I have been here about a year and a half and when I first came here the Minister of Finance and the President of the Treasury Board of the day were talking about what proved to be a phony program of cutbacks in expenditure. It turned out that they were not talking about cutbacks in expenditures at all. Then we went through the period when they cooked the books at the time of the last election and then disclosed quite freely when the election was over substantially higher estimates for the year. We then had the October budget with vast increases in taxes and the projection that inflation would be brought under control. Now we have the recent budget in which the minister admits that the October budget was a failure. So there is no confidence in the financial policies of this government. After all this talk we still have an unacceptable rate of inflation accompanied by an unacceptable degree of unemployment in the country.
[DOT] (3:20 p.m.)
Inflation, sir, is not just something we talk about; it is something that affects people. Consider for a moment the effect of an inflation rate of 4 per cent per year on the ordinary people of this country. Consider the effect on pensioners. How does inflation affect the pensioner's real standard of living? Consider the effect of inflation on the real purchasing power of those who receive family allowances. Consider also the terrible effect inflation has on the poor in this country. In addition, inflation increases income taxes without the authorization of parliament. It lowers exemptions incomes of people very substantially. It inflates incomes and therefore increases the actual rate of taxation of Canadians who pay additional hundreds of millions of dollars every year. Not only must we keep in mind that we pay this regressive 2 per cent social development tax which the minister imposed in October as well as other tax increases the minister imposed openly; we must also keep in mind that in every year in which there is substantial inflation, as at present, our people pay additional taxes which have not been authorized by parliament.
The Budget-Mr. Stanfield
The minister boasts of his surplus. That surplus is accounted for by the speed-up in the collection of taxes from corporations, by the fact that a number of provinces will not participate in the medicare program for the full year and by the unauthorized tax increase which is a result of inflation. What Minister of Finance collecting increased taxes consequent upon the increases imposed last October as well as increased amounts of tax money accruing as a result of the inflation taking place under his policies could fail to produce a surplus?

In addition, the minister keeps the lid on family allowances and allows old age pensioners inadequate compensation with which to meet increased living costs. Not only does the minister keep the lid on such payments but he also says to the provinces. "We will not pay attention to your priorities or payments. The answer is no, no, no. Go back and attend to your own problems and pay no attention at all to the recommendations on the Economic Council of Canada with regard to adequate programs concerning the poor." What has the minister to boast about under these circumstances when he produces a surplus? All these tax increases will burden economically hundreds of thousands of people in Canada.
I believe the minister tried to suggest in his budget that he was not increasing taxes. Of course he is. He is extending the 3 per cent surcharge even though the government solemnly assured the people of Canada it would be eliminated at the end of this year.

The Budget-Mr. Stanfield the government is increasing taxation, no matter what view the government or the Minister of Finance may take of the matter. At the same time, of course, there have been increased charges for services provided by the government. Also, as a result of inflation, taxation is constantly increasing. The minister is promoting inflation.
We have heard much talk about inflation. On March 29, 1966, the Minister of Finance of that day, who is now Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Sharp), is reported to have said in the house:
Mr. Speaker, if we do not by one means or another succeed in moderating the increase in aggregate expenditures this year the most immediate penalty we shall suffer is an inflationary increase in prices.
That was said in March, 1966. On December 19, 1966, that minister is reported to have said:
If some moderation in demands with inflationary consequences does not occur we may well find it necessary to impose sufficient fiscal restraint upon the economy as a whole to check them.
Then on June 1, 1967, that minister is reported to have said:
The most unsatisfactory aspect of the 1967 situation in Canada, as in many other countries, is the continuing upward movements in costs and prices .. . the rate of increase of consumer prices is more than we can tolerate on a continuing basis.
We now hear these pious statements twice a year. In November, 1967, the Minister of Finance is reported to have made the following statement:
We must bring to an end the present round of inflationary price and cost increases, and move to a situation in which all Canadians can work and buy and bargain and invest in the expectation that their money over the years will maintain its real value.
On March 6,, 1968, he is reported to have said:
It seems quite evident to me that our first priority in economic policy now must be to achieve greater stability in prices and costs.
Then we had a change of actors, but the role they played remained the same. The present Minister of Finance is reported to have said on October 22, 1968:
In the broad field of economic policy, the most urgent need now is to check further the continuing increase in prices and living costs.
Again, on June 3 this pleasant and optimistic Minister of Finance repeated the theme. 
We are getting budget speeches twice a year now. He is reported to have said:
There can be no question that the number one priority in economic policy today must be to deploy all available forces-public and private-more aggressively than ever in the battle against inflation in Canada.
For how long must we listen to such statements from Liberal Ministers of Finance? Four years ago the Liberal government first decided that inflation had gotten out of hand in Canada; yet we still hear these platitudes. They still want to reassess everything. Four years ago the Liberal government first waved over our heads the axe of spending cuts. They are still waving the axe.

subtopic: THE BUDGET

speechtext: That was a hoax.

subtopic: THE BUDGET
subsubtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The axe is still being waved around somewhere over there, and I do not think that the supply of band-aids has been overly strained. What has the Liberal government been doing during the last three or four years of concern? The taxpayers of Canada know what it has been doing. We have lost count of all the tax increases we have suffered from in the past few years. These were tax increases the government imposed in the name of fighting inflation. The taxpayer wonders what is happening when he sees his personal income tax boosted to 164 per cent above the 1962-66 level. This year, sir, it is estimated that Canadians will pay 32 per cent more in personal income taxes. I suggest this sort of thing cannot be allowed to continue. We have had four years of so-called anti-inflationary policy and tax increases and still the Minister of Finance rises in his place and says that inflation will not slacken in this country this year. The Minister of Finance in fact is relying on inflation to balance his budget. I ask him how much of that 32 per cent increase in personal income tax this year is directly attributable to the inflation taking place during 1969? Wages and salaries would not be increasing so fast if we did not have an inflation which cuts the heart out of the spending power of the ordinary individual's income.
[DOT] (3:30 p.m.)
Consumer prices are going up at a rate of 4.7 per cent a year. That was the figure from May to May. A man has to earn at least that much more just to keep up. In fact, he has to earn more. For example, he does not enjoy any adjustment in his income tax deductions to allow for inflation. He just pays more. A married man with two children and an
June 10, 1969

income of $5,000,. receiving an increase of 4.7 per cent which is just enough to match the consumer price increase, would still be penalized by about $50. Real income is no higher but the people are paying a substantially higher tax which this government imposes secretly without any parliamentary authorization. As a result of these things we have the balanced budget about which the minister boasts. We wonder, Mr. Speaker, we wonder.
No one questions the importance of fighting inflation adequately and effectively. I have said many times that the longer this process goes on the less and less we will have to fight it effectively, and more and more vested interests will develop in favour of continued inflation. The chairman of the Prices and Incomes Commission says it is a mistake to bet on continued inflation. The Minister of Finance is betting on it. He not only bets on it, he predicts it. He is not only predicting it but he is counting on it to continue to produce the surplus that he is predicting. He is betting on continued inflation, Mr. Speaker. There can be no doubt about the manifold injustice that inflation is perpetrating in Canada.
Are the minister's proposals effective? Can we reasonably expect the methods proposed by the minister to succeed? I reminded hon. members a few moments ago about what we have heard from successive Ministers of Finance in the past four years-the same old thing, increased taxes to fight inflation. It has not succeeded. Inflation has continued. In fact, inflation has escalated. What new methods has the minister proposed? He has made a proposal to defer depreciation regarding commercial construction in certain centres in Canada. He has proposed that the Kennedy Round tariff reductions be implemented immediately rather than phased in over a number of years. I say to the minister that these proposals are interesting but I do not think they amount to very much in total.
What is the purpose of the minister in presenting this budgetary statement? Is his purpose psychological? Is his purpose to convince the people of Canada that this government is determined to conquer inflation? Is this his purpose? Was it for this reason the minister projected in the future a prospect of continuing present taxes? Was it for this reason he placed emphasis upon predicting the budgetary surplus and protecting it against those who might try to raid it? If this was his purpose, we must ask ourselves whether the minister has succeeded.
The Budget-Mr. Stanfield
Has the minister convinced the Canadian public this government is going to win the fight against inflation? It seems not, as far as I can judge. It may be this failure to convince the public is not the fault of the Minister of Finance. As the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) suggested yesterday in connection with another matter, it may be the press that is at fault. They may have failed to carry conviction in this instance as in the other.
It is little wonder the public remains sceptical because what the minister told us about in the way of hard fact represented a continuation of failure. We must expect a low level of public acceptance and confidence in view of the misleading record of the government and its continuing record of bumbling. I wonder whether the Minister of Finance, like some others, could have an image problem to contend with? If he has, Mr. Speaker, it would be little wonder because we have had continued inflation and continued tax increases to fight inflation year after year.
I hope the minister read the government's own white paper on the subject of inflation which was tabled in the house last December. What some of us have been saying for some time is there in black and white, that the traditional methods employed by this government to fight inflation have not succeeded. It was clear to those who presented that white paper that the traditional methods had failed to achieve the aims of the government, that is, to provide reasonable stability of prices while providing a reasonably satisfactory degree of employment in the country. The government's record has been condemned in its own white paper. That white paper recommended the appointment of a Prices and Incomes Commission. I said at the time this was like putting a popgun in the hands of our troops. Lord knows, the white paper was slow enough in being presented in the first place. It was produced in December. It could have been written by two or three people sitting around for two or three days. We waited from June until December to get that white paper.
The only real recommendation the white paper made was the appointment of the Prices and Incomes Commission. We do not have the commission yet despite the fact that we question the minister responsible day after day, week after week, month after month. How can the Minister of Finance or the government expect anybody in Canada to take seriously suggestions that they are determined in their efforts to fight inflation when they have not acted on a very simple and
June 10, 1969

The Budget-Mr. Stanfield easy recommendation in their own white paper?
For three or four years the Economic Council of Canada has been recommending the establishment in this country with the government's help, of an independent forecasting unit. I think it should be apparent to the Minister of Finance that no one needs an independent forecasting unit more than he in view of the discrepancy in a few months between what he predicted in October and what we now have. The Economic Council of Canada says a forecasting unit to forecast relatively short term trends would, among other things, enable the government to present and develop policies related to conditions likely to develop and not conditions the Minister of Finance may imagine are likely to develop. Why has the government not been prepared to accept the recommendations of the Economic Council of Canada and co-operate with that very respectable body, the Private Planning Association, by establishing a forecasting unit? Why is there this stubborn determination to tie one hand behind its back with regard to developing adequate programs? Why continue this game of blindman's bluff which the minister persists in continuing? It is a perfectly simple, straightforward recommendation that the government has refused to act upon. That being so, how can members of the government expect any of us to take them seriously?
[DOT] (3:40 p.m.)
We have been talking about inflationary psychology. I remember the minister's predecessor talking about inflationary psychology in this country. There have been four years of talk, four years of higher taxation each year, four years of inflation each year. The minister's forecasts cannot carry any conviction. He expects that the inflation is going to continue. If he expects it to continue the people of Canada will expect it to continue and they will be making preparations for this in their forward contracts, whether they be labour contracts or any other type of contracts. In those circumstances, what chance have we of bringing inflation down to an acceptable level?
We must adopt different approaches. I do not mean that we should abandon fiscal and monetary measures. Of course we must have them, but the government's own white paper in December last said that these measures are inadequate. For a couple of years past the

O.E.C.D. has recommended that the government start to work toward an incomes policy. The governor of the Bank of Canada has made the same recommendation.
, Surely the government must realize by this time that you do not halt inflation just by creating unemployment. This was the policy of the minister's predecessor who said in this house that if it was necessary he would create some slack in the economy and unemployment, and this the government proceeded to do. We have now got the unemployment but we have more inflation than ever before.
Some new methods must be adopted to reinforce our attack on these problems. Ever since I came into this house I have urged that the government screw up its courage a bit and mobilize the Canadian people to fight inflation by getting together with business, labour and the community at large and developing guidelines, not as a permanent solution but as a way of breaking out of the vicious circle in which the Minister of Finance and the government have placed Canada.

-were substantially responsible for the United States doing a far better job for a number of years in controlling inflation than Canada did, and those guidelines broke down when they were not backed up by adequate, appropriate fiscal policies just because Congress would not act. Lord knows, by contrast, Mr. Speaker, the minister has got through enough tax increases in this country. I recommend this very earnestly as an interim measure. I recommend that the government seek the co-operation and help of the Canadian people. I recommend that it convince them that Canada is going to break out of this inflationary psychology, is going to fight it effectively, and that the government is going to stop fooling around year after year with tax increases. This at least would give the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs time enough to get his Incomes and Prices Commission set up. If we give the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs a year's breathing space he might get it set up. But are we going to wait around for years and
June 10. 1969

years for the members of the Prices and Incomes Commission to recommend policies to the government? Are we going to keep on raising taxes each year and seeing more and more inflation? Again, Mr. Speaker, why will the Minister of Finance not do something about establishing the forecasting unit recommended by the Economic Council of Canada and by the Private Planning Association? There is not one possible reason he can advance for this failure except the inertia of the government.
The minister's methods are not only failing with regard to inflation, putting a cruel and unjust burden upon the poor and the unfortunate, but the policies he is resorting to more and more all the time, policies of taxation applied uniformly across the country, are creating unemployment, are creating unnecessary hardship, are creating unnecessary waste of human resources in Canada. These policies are not only ineffective but they are brutal. These fiscal and monetary policies applied uniformly across the country depress the areas of slow growth such as the province of Quebec, the Atlantic provinces and other parts of the country.
As my distinguished colleague, the hon. member for Carleton-Charlotte (Mr. Flemming), said a few years ago, it is like giving castor oil to everybody whether they need it or not. Unquestionably the Minister of Finance is increasing the degree of economic disparity in Canada. Unquestionably he is very substantially increasing the difficulties of the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion (Mr. Marchand) through these fiscal policies that he is imposing, these uniformly applied tight money policies that he is developing.
A few weeks ago when he was among the people affected in New Brunswick the Prime Minister recognized that these policies were working hardships on them. What did he say to those people when he was among them? He said, "We are going to increase our expenditures down here to offset this." But what did he and the Minister of Finance do when he came back to Ottawa? Nothing, Mr. Speaker.
The program of the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion is a long-range one. He himself admits that it will take years for the program to get off the ground. In the meantime the Minister of Finance is putting the economy in the slow growth regions of Canada more firmly on the skids. There can be no doubt about the dampening effect of his fiscal and monetary policies, and there can be no doubt that they ought to be offset. It is in the

The Budget-Mr. Stanfield national as well as the regional interest to do this.
There are no inflationary pressures in those unfortunate parts of the country. What they do have is idle human resources. On the other hand, a great deal has to be done in those parts of Canada to prepare for the work of the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion, as that minister himself would be the first to agree. There is the question of the level of growth-related government services provided in those areas. There is the question of an adequate economic infrastructure.
Hon. gentlemen opposite may refer to the new program for Prince Edward Island and to the ARDA program adopted in New Brunswick. Mr. Speaker, my impression is that the New Brunswick program is more or less as flat as a pancake, and the P.E.I. program has not yet started and will take some time. In any event, much more is required if the growth concept advocated by the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion is to be implemented.
This sort of thing ought to have been planned in ways which would not add to inflationary pressures in Canada. There has been plenty of time for the planning. At the time of his budget last October the Minister of Finance knew what the effect of his fiscal measures must be in these areas. He must have known that the money supply had to be tightened up, that the Bank of Canada could not go on increasing the supply of money at the rate it had during the previous year, substantially to enable the Minister of Finance to sell his bonds. This simply could not continue.
[DOT] (3:50 p.m.)
There was plenty of time for planning. The most charitable thing to say is that the minister did not look very far ahead. But even so, are we to move through a whole fiscal year with these depressing effects on our wheat farmers, for example? Are we to go through a whole fiscal year with the economy, or a substantial part of it, being more and more depressed month after month? The Minister of Finance will say that he has inserted selective methods of controlling inflation such as his deferral of depreciation allowances on commercial buildings in certain centres. In all sincerity I wish to compliment the minister on a matter of principle for recognizing the desirability of the use of selective measures to control inflation and for recognizing, I think for the first time in any formal way, that inflationary pressures are not uniform throughout the country.
9944	COMMONS
The Budget-Mr. Stanfield
So far as the effectiveness, the appropriateness and workability of this proposal is concerned, that is another matter about which a number of members have had something to say. I wish to emphasize that I approve in principle what the minister has recognized. I want to emphasize also, however, that this measure, even if it does have the effect of slowing down commercial construction in these centres, will not do anything to encourage the development of the slow growth areas. It will not do anything to obviate the depressive effect of the general fiscal and monetary policies of the minister. I suggest that we need flexible fiscal and monetary approaches. I am not suggesting a different interest rate for the banking system in different parts of the country. But I believe we can achieve a flexible system of brakes to be applied to credit in different parts of the country. I have argued this for a dozen years. My point of view now seems to have some respectable support.
I understand the minister is to meet with the bank presidents later this month. I hope he will urge them to apply this policy in the Canadian banking system. I think this can be done without adding to the difficulties of the banks, because only a small demand out of their total credit arises in these regions of slow growth. I sincerely urge that the minister take a progressive step forward by encouraging the banks to take this step which would mitigate to some extent the other policies proposed by the minister. I can understand the minister's concern about protecting his surplus. He will be raided from all sides. But certainly the fight against regional disparity is supposed to be a top priority of this government. Certainly his policies in general are deepening regional disparity and deepening the difficulties the government will have in overcoming this disparity, as well as creating hardships for many thousands of Canadians.
I suggest there are also offsetting factors, particularly when one considers the multiplier effect of the appropriate expenditures in these areas such as those in connection with unemployment and welfare. They could increase the government's tax take in those areas. There would certainly by no means be a complete net loss to the treasury. I say in all sincerity that the present policies as proposed are callous and damaging to the national as well as regional interests.
There is another area, the cash position of the western wheat farmers, which I believe to be an emergency position. There are other

DEBATES	June 10, 1969
problems for the farmers of this country but I believe this represents a real emergency. Yet we see nothing but vacillation and obscurity on the part of the government when we ask whether anything is to be done. Is the government waiting until the recess? There have been a number of proposals made such as the two-price system, assistance through acreage payments and the payment of some of the charges for storage on the farm.
I realize there are some objections to some of these proposals. There can be objections to any proposal which might be put forward about anything. But the difficulty in which these people find themselves is beyond their control. Their difficulties are not the result of their own mistakes or judgment. These are not difficulties in which people have become involved because they are inefficient. I understand that many of the best farmers in western Canada are seriously short of cash. There is an emergency. I say to the government: "Do not let these people go down the drain. Stop fooling around.

speechtext:
I suppose the minister will talk about the advantage of his tariff cuts to the people in the west. I think the tariff cuts are fine to the extent that they increase competition and to the extent that they tend to inhibit price increases. Some say they will not have any effect in that direction. I am prepared to agree with the minister they probably will have some tendency to fight price increases and bring some prices down. Let us assume that.
In addition, the effect on Canadian industry is difficult to measure. I really seriously query whether the minister does know or took the trouble to find out what the effect on industry will be. Will it have the effect of bringing into immediate operation the reductions which have been announced to take effect a few years hence? I doubt that he knows how the effect will be distributed across the country. Master as the Minister of Finance is of non sequiturs, I never expected him to argue that industries would get in no difficulty as a result of this surprise announcement just because they were able to adjust in an orderly way to an open and disclosed reduction to take effect over a number of years. I suggest that this kind of sudden change in the rules without warning-I might as well be blunt about it since we are face to face-is stupid and unnecessary.
June 10, 1969	COMMONS
I do not claim that all Canadian manufacturing industry is efficient and I do not object at all to persistent and rational exposure of Canadian industry to pressure of competition with a view to increasing its efficiency and encouraging it where necessary as well as restructuring the industry. But this process in any event is difficult for industry. The adjustment is difficult. The process is painful and it involves risks because ordinarily it involves increased investment to achieve a result which cannot be certain. Above all, it requires confidence. A man who faces this kind of increased competition and who makes the necessary investments and adjustments must have confidence.
[DOT] (4:00 p.m.)
The sudden arbitrary action of the Minister of Finance in announcing this kind of change without notice can only be unsettling, destructive and have the effect of weakening the confidence which the Canadian businessman needs. I must say to the minister that Canadian business people cannot now count on what the government is likely to do. The government announced it would eliminate the 3 per cent surtax at the end of this year. It has abandoned that commitment. The government announced in the house that there would be an orderly reduction of tariffs under GATT over a number of years and then suddenly, without any notice, told us that as of tomorrow morning the rules would be changed. There is no need for this sort of thing. This sort of surprise and shock does not encourage a maximum restructuring of Canadian industry. It simply introduces a further element of irrationality into the process, namely, that possibly arbitrary decisions by this government will come at an increasing rate.
Furthermore, there is no compensating opening of trading areas to Canadian industry. Surely if this government knew what it was about, and if it was prepared to concede more than it did at the time of the GATT treaty, it would have been able to get more in return at that time. It would have been able to open doors. This is another example of these sudden switches in policy for short term effects, not really related in any rational way to long term planning. This is gimmickry, and that is all it is, of a very uncertain type.
There was very heavy emphasis put on the need for the restructuring of Canadian industry and increasing its efficiency. Those who talk about this process do not give adequate attention to access of Canadian industry 29180-629
DEBATES	9945
The Budget-Mr. Stanfield to markets on terms of reasonable competition with their competitors. I think it is a very questionable belief that Canada can restructure its industry and develop substantive industry in the technological era, with all the necessary economics of scale, by relying simply upon multilateral arrangements. Even if it could, this kind of arbitrary announcement by the minister is not a necessary part of that process.
It is fair to say that Sweden has been exposed to international competition for a long time and has developed highly specialized industries. Sweden is part of the Outer Seven and has tariff free access to a market of some $100 billion. Even though it has access to a free market of this size it is trying, like Britain, to get into the Common Market. Yet Canada is trying to develop this kind of sophisticated and modern industry with free access to a market of less than 25 million people.
How can we be expected to share the same kind of pressures that affect Sweden and Britain? Is Canada different or distinctive in this respect? Are we not going to be subject to the same pressures? Does this not involve the encouraging of the restructuring of Canadian industry by increasing competition through lowering tariffs? If we are going to compete successfully in this world we must have access to necessary markets on terms comparable with those of our competitors. A firm in the United States has tariff free access to a market of 200 million people. The same applies to an industry in the Common Market where there are no tariffs. Having regard to the exposure of Canadian industry to increased competition, this must of necessity be only a part of an adequate program to encourage the efficiency and development of Canadian industry.
Surely the Canadian concessions the minister announced could have been used to open some doors which in turn could be well used by the industry of Canada, thus allowing them a good chance to compete internationally. Surely at the very least these concessions could have been used to help Canadians involved in the oil industry, and other Canadians in marketing their fish or wheat. It is difficult to understand the arbitrary stand and processes of thought of the Minister of Finance. When he was giving something away he did not even take the trouble to get something in return.
In his budget address the Minister of Finance made reference to the very crucial
9946	COMMONS
The Budget-Mr. Stanfield question of federal-provincial fiscal relations. He stated that he was "encouraged by the evidence of closer consultation and co-ordination in fiscal policy".
He congratulated the provinces on their "most strenuous efforts... to improve or maintain budgetary balance." Most of the provinces do deserve hearty congratulations on their budgetary efforts and their willingness to accept a share of the responsibility for the double-barrelled battle against inflation and unemployment. This, in some cases at least, required extremely difficult political decisions under difficult circumstances.
What is cause for extreme concern on the part of all Canadians is the extent to which the provincial budgetary efforts have been made even more difficult by the irresponsible activity of the present federal government. A brief glance at some of the budget addresses made by provincial treasurers this spring is enough to convince anyone that the process of federal-provincial consultation and co-operation is not quite as harmonious as the smiling Minister of Finance would have us believe. At least he smiled at the time he said it, which was just as well, I think.
The federal government seems to consider itself exempt from such limitations. The most glaring example of the unwillingness of the federal government to abide by the spirit, if not by the letter, of the agreements and arrangements with the provinces was the implementation of the regressive social development tax, and doing it in such a way that it was not shared. This tax measure is regrettable not only because it is regressive but also because it callously excludes the hard-pressed provinces from their normal share of revenues derived from taxes on personal income.
This federal action was denounced in almost every provincial budget this spring, and justifiably so. While the denial of legitimate revenues to the provinces is a serious offence, the real danger is that such arbitrary federal actions will completely destroy the commonly accepted norms of fair play that are the real basis of the binding effect of agreements between governments which are all sovereign in their own spheres. That this is a danger was clearly hinted at by Finance Minister DesBrisay of New Brunswick when he referred to the social development tax in these words, which I am sure are well imprinted on the mind of the Minister of Finance:
Ottawa's response has been that each province must establish its own ... taxation policies within the existing federal-provincial arrangements.

DEBATES	June 10, 1969
I regret to say . . . that in our opinion the federal government by its own subsequent actions has made it exceedingly difficult for the provinces to follow that advice.
I should not have to paint a picture for hon. members of the results which would inevitably follow if federal actions made this type of feeling too widespread.
However, what is most worrisome for the future of federal-provincial relations is the fact that the social development tax is only the most visible example of a more general attitude on the part of this government. It appears that the minister's and the government's concept of consultation and co-operation is a one-way street involving provincial accommodation to federal decisions unilaterally taken. Such an attitude can only fan feelings of distrust in the provincial capitals of this country.
Anybody who reads the provincial budget speeches will see ample evidence of provincial disenchantment with the federal attitude. For instance, the uncertainties and disruptions generated by this kind of unilateral knife-wielding by the minister in Ottawa on important share-cost programs have been roundly denounced. In case anybody should think I am referring to people who might have a political bias, let me refer briefly to a statement by the provincial treasurer of Saskatchewan. Mr. Steuart observed, and this is a pretty serious assertion:
I am convinced our national unity demands a higher level of integrity than now exists in federal-provincial fiscal negotiations.
I would not like to have someone say that about me if I were the Minister of Finance, particularly someone I thought was a friend of mine. Mr. Steuart claimed that "at times Ottawa seems to be trying to hoodwink us."
* (4:10 p.m.)
