speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as I travel throughout my constituency of Halton I meet more and more people who are becoming increasingly concerned about the rising cost of living. They ask where all this is leading to because they realize that the answer, so far as they are concerned, is not to be found in an annual increase in the pay envelope so that they as individuals and as heads of families can meet these rising costs. Thinking people-and I include many people who are connected with the labour movement whom I have met-realize that somewhere there must be an end to this trend, and it may not be a happy one.
An increase in a person's wages or salary under present-day conditions can only be a temporary cure. The average man will be at the same place a year from now as he is today, without enough money to buy the things he needs or would like to buy because in the intervening time living costs have increased in too many cases to a greater degree than the increase in money he received. Therefore I would like to look at this question of inflation from the standpoint of both the individual and the government I would like to look at what inflation is doing to the individual and what it is doing to the country as a whole.
29180-629i
June 10, 1969

The Budget-Mr. Whiting
Of course we realize that wages and salaries are not in themselves a cause of inflation. In fact, increased wages and salaries need not contribute to inflation if they are related to productivity. In Canada, as in other countries, inflation is affected by world prices, government spending and monetary policies.
As I have said, many of my constituents have asked where this inflation is leading us. As a member of the Standing Committee on Regional Development I have focused my attention especially on the effects of inflation on the Canadian way of life and on what it is doing to the people who are not in a position to receive an annual increase in income. This takes in a very large group of people and exceeds in numbers those who have to live on fixed incomes such as the elderly and those living on pensions. There are also large numbers of people in many areas of Canada who have no way of increasing their incomes.
One of the reasons for this is found in the centralization of economic activity that is taking place today. People are being drawn to the larger urban centres. As these urban centres grow, so do the markets that surround them, thus creating an economic climate that lures an ever-increasing number of industries to establish within a radius of these areas. Business establishments located beyond the perimeters of such areas and markets find it difficult to compete unless they have some natural resource or an asset from which they can benefit.
Thus we find areas in Canada where the incomes of the people either remain stationary or decrease while the general cost of goods and services rises. Because of this present and growing disparity in activity, and what I have already seen as a member of the Regional Development Committee on our recent trip to certain areas of western Canada, I was most encouraged to see that the Minister of Finance is aware of the effect that inflation is having on these disadvantaged areas, and the government has made the program of the new Department of Regional Economic Expansion a major commitment.
[DOT] (4:20 p.m.)
The fight against inflation and programs for regional expansion must go hand in hand. Otherwise, inflation will be a constant drawback and restraint to the success of these programs no matter how well-intentioned and how well-conceived they may be.
Of course, all is not sweetness and light in those areas where Canada is enjoying its most

active economic expansion. Inflation has had its effect on housing and this is one of our great national problems. The net result is that many men who are able to find jobs are not able to find housing accommodation at a cost which will permit them to enjoy a standard of living which includes a good environment.
Although housing legislation was discussed in the house in the past week, I would like to make a few comments at this time on the subject. In spite of statistics which show that this year will likely be a record year in terms of housing starts, we will continue to have a very serious problem on our hands until such time as the people of this country feel that they have adequate housing. As long as people are unhappy with their present housing circumstances and are unable, for whatever reason, to move to something better, I believe we have an obligation to exert whatever effort and energies we can to improve housing conditions.
Many people, including builders, economists, scholars and home owners, have called the present situation a housing crisis, a money crisis, a land crisis, a mortgage crisis. Might I add, Mr. Speaker, there is also a people crisis involved in certain aspects of this problem. There is no doubt in my mind that if the right people co-operate at all three levels of government the present housing dilemma can and will be solved.
I am very pleased with the recent legislation introduced by the government which includes a move to allow N.H.A. mortgage rates to be reviewed every five years. This will do much to bring banks and trust companies into the mortgage market in a bigger way. Experience with conventional mortgage loans has proven five-year terms to be very appropriate. I think we are also wise to make more funds available for direct loans and generally to encourage more funds into Canadian mortgages. However, it is imperative we realize that providing mortgage money is not the only answer. We must look also to land costs, building codes, construction methods, new products and labour efficiency if we are to succeed.
We must, I think, be acutely aware of those who earn $5,000 to $6,000 or less per year. We must also think of the young married couples just starting out. Above all, it is our duty to see that the older generation who have already made their contribution to this country will, in their declining years, have peace of mind in the knowledge that adequate housing is available to them. We owe this to those
June 10, 1969	COMMONS
of our senior citizens who through the years have given service to this country.
It is, therefore, my contention that we must look at housing not only in the light of the inflation which has taken place within the industry itself, but also at the effect inflation is having on the entire economy of the country and the living standards of the Canadian people.
It has been pointed out that Canadian exports amount to $17 billion annually. This represents one-quarter of the gross national product. Obviously, exports are a cornerstone of the Canadian economic structure. A fluctuation of any proportion can affect the well-being of our citizens, as it affects government income and government programs. It is, therefore, essential that everything possible be done to protect and promote our exports. What is actually being done about this both privately and by government?
Let us look first at what the government is doing. I think Canadians should realize that some of the measures taken by this government reveal a considerable degree of political courage which is essential at this time. It is somewhat akin to going to the doctor and having him tell you, "This is going to hurt." You are not very happy with him at the time but you know the treatment is going to result to your benefit.
I	refer to the recent increase in postal rates imposed by the Minister of Communications (Mr. Kierans) and to the tax on airline tickets included in the budget. Both these measures indicate the desire of the government to place public services on a businesslike basis to ensure, where possible, that people are asked to pay for services rendered to them rather than making those services a burden on the public at large.
In his budget address the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) indicated the intention of the government to live within its income for the first time in 12 years. This is welcome news to me and to my constituents. I represent a constituency embracing a community which pays more per capita into the federal coffers than any other municipality in Canada. In fact it is my belief that this statement could apply to my whole riding. Naturally, my constituents are concerned with the manner in which government money is spent. In this respect I doubt that they differ from the constituents of any other hon. member. When, for example, the Auditor General's report was published, the press in Halton took a good hard look at it. In fact one newspaper
DEBATES	9949
The Budget-Mr. Whiting devoted a whole week to printing excerpts from this report and commenting on them. Some of these comments were not too complimentary, and justifiably so.
I think the time has come when we must stop thinking that laxity in the supervision of the spending of public funds can be regarded as an acceptable, government practice. Each and every member of this house who serves on various committees must take it upon himself to scrutinize the manner in which public moneys are spent. If he fails, then every Member of Parliament must be prepared to face an aroused public. I believe a start has been made in this direction, judging by the aggressive manner in which the Public Accounts Committee is looking into the way in which certain expenditures have been made in the past year. I would like to see the same efficiency and diligence as is displayed by the federal government in the collection of taxes-and I am happy to see the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Cote) present in the house-applied to its spending of the Canadian taxpayers' money.
I should like to make one further reference to the fight against inflation which the Minister of Finance called the No. 1 priority in economic policy in the course of his budget statement. A few minutes ago I pointed out that exports are the cornerstone of our economy and that we must do everything in our power to see they are not jeopardized. It has been said on many occasions that if the price spiral continues it is within the realm of possibility that we shall price ourselves out of the export market altogether in many areas. This would immediately lead to mass unemployment for many Canadians and a serious decline in economic activity. I stated at the beginning of my remarks that many people have asked: where is this inflationary spiral leading? I think that is the answer if we are not capable of stopping it.
[DOT] (4:30 p.m.)
It is essential that we reverse the cost spiral. A good start has been made in the budget by the immediate implementation of the Kennedy Round of tariff reductions. The next step is action on the part of Canadian manufacturers. Many manufacturing companies have public relations departments or public relations advisers, and all are concerned with their public image. May I suggest to them that they focus public attention on their ability to improve efficiency and productivity in order to lower consumer prices. By doing so with honesty and sincerity of intention, the
June 10, 1969

The Budget-Mrs. Maclnnis constant and ever-recurring demand for increased salaries and wages would lose much of its validity. The point to bear in mind is that it is not just the dollar in one's pocket but how much that dollar can buy. If we in Canada can keep our prices competitive, we can enjoy the greatest prosperity, industrial peace and the highest standard of living in the world.

subtopic: THE BUDGET
subsubtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there are some good features in this budget and these have been detailed for us by government members. However, I feel that the budget cannot be judged simply by its good features. We have all heard of the curate's egg, which was good in spots. But the effect of the curate's egg was not good, even though it may have had some good spots. This budget must be judged according to its total effect.
I am not going to deal with the good spots today but with the effect of the budget, as I see it, on the majority of the Canadian people. Undoubtedly some people must have faith and confidence in this budget; otherwise it would not have been framed as it is. But a good many people I meet do not have faith and confidence in the budget, and I might point out that I do meet a good many people. The people I meet are becoming worried, and badly worried.
These people see a government with a big over-all majority. Remember, we were told that we had to have a government with a big over-all majority in order to get things done. These people see a government with wide legislative jurisdiction able to pass the legislation it desires to pass. They see a government with taxing powers apparently unrestrained and unlimited. They are assured that the government has access to the brightest minds in the country, in the civil service and among economists.
This government has repeatedly told the voters since the last election that it has been gearing up to get its machinery going so as to bring about a just society in this country. Since the budget has been brought down and all of this machinery has been set in motion, these people who have waited expectantly for results are seeing a government that apparently is completely unable to curb the steady rise in the cost of living, a government, indeed, that says that inflation is inevitable and will continue, a government which, so far from being able to do away with and prevent pockets of poverty, is apparently unable to


prevent these pockets of poverty from growing into regions of ruin.
These people see a government that is unable to prevent the erosion of our economy by unemployment and replace unemployment by the steady growth of productive industries and services in this country. They see a government that is unable to supply hope for people old and young across the land. Worst of all, they see in this budget a government that is repeating the same techniques that led to our present miseries, making the same mistakes over and over again in every field I could mention.
I believe that the people are not only concerned but very seriously worried. Increasing numbers of people have told me during the last while that they are beginning to be worried that the economy of this country is rapidly getting out of control, that we have a government that is quite unable to handle the situation, a government that is allowing things to drift and which cannot do anything about it.
Since I come from the province of British Columbia I would compare this situation to a forest fire that is raging across the country, the forest fire of inflation that means a higher cost of living and lower income. The government is dousing this forest fire with gasoline while at the same time telling the people that it has the very latest in water bombers, that it has a wonderful crew of economists and civil servants, that it has the last word in techniques, such as white papers, boards, commissions, task forces and all the rest. It also has the best gasoline to be had in the whole market. These are the suspicions that people are beginning to have. They are content to give the government an "e" for effort, but the consequences for the Canadian people are terrible and are becoming worse.
Let me detail very briefly the kind of people who are being menaced by this budget, those for whom this budget is a bitter disappointment, not only a bitter disappointment on paper but a budget that hurts them in reality.
First of all, I would mention our old age pensioners and other people who have retired such as superannuated public servants, as well as people living on small fixed incomes which were determined before the cost of living rose to the level it is today. Typical of these people is the old age pensioner group. The cost of living rose 4 per cent last year while their pensions went up 2 per cent. The gap will be even wider this year since the
June 10, 1969	COMMONS
latest available index of the cost of living shows a rise of 4.7 per cent while pensions are tied to a statutory 2 per cent increase. We are told that the forecast is that the cost of living may drop in the immediate future, but the record so far gives no hope for that. Even the government does not claim there will be anything but an increase in the cost of living as we go along into the future.
My colleague, the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) outlined the other day what has happened to old age pensioners since the government gave them the guaranteed income supplement. A great many of the elderly recipients of old age security who also get the supplement, which means that they cannot get less than $105 a month, plus cost of living increases, are now placed in the position where they are taxable because of the supplement. So in actual fact they are worse off as a result of receiving the supplement than they were before.
This is why people are so alarmed at this government's incompetence, if I can use a kind word, though I could use words much less kind. The government is giving something with one hand and taking it away with the other. It is not that its right hand does not know what its left hand is doing but that the government hopes that the person who receives a few cents in one pocket does not feel a few more cents very skilfully being taken out of his other pocket at the same time. That is the first group I wanted to mention which is actually being menaced by this government as a result of the spread getting wider between what they have to live on and what they have to pay out.
[DOT] (4:40 p.m.)
The second group I want to mention is the young people of this country. The minister may tell us that young students can obtain student loans. I will not enter into an argument on this point. Often such loans become mortgages on our young people's futures. Many young people are unwilling to assume obligations they cannot pay off. Consequently they are reluctant to borrow money for their higher education. Also, notwithstanding the pious statements coming from the government front benches, students across Canada are finding it extremely difficult to obtain jobs this summer. In the Vancouver area last year half the young people looking for summer jobs did not find any. Undoubtedly the student unemployment situation in Vancouver will become worse this year, and what is true of Vancouver is true of other centres
DEBATES	9951
The Budget-Mrs. Maclnnis across Canada. So what is the sense in the minister saying to our young people, "Take out a loan and mortgage your futures in the name of higher education even though you will not be able to find a job and thus liquidate your debt." This reminds me of robbing Peter to pay Paul. You are putting something into one pocket and taking it from the other.
Our veterans are the third group of persons I wish to talk about. They have inadequate allowances. For months and months they have been led to believe that veterans allowances are to be increased. The government told them that as soon as the Woods report was handed down veterans living allowances would be increased. Well, that has not happened. No doubt many hon. members have received letters from veterans on this subject.
I know that veterans and their families are suffering. Now the government tells us that veterans allowances will not be increased during the present session. Apparently the government wishes to present us with a fait accompli by having a white paper ready when the Woods report has been studied. The government wishes to prepare its legislation and does not wish veterans to know the contents of that legislation ahead of time. If we had participatory democracy in the true sense the government would have asked veterans and their organizations to appear this session before the Standing Committee on Veterans Affairs and make representations. The government could then act on those representations. That has not happened.
Clearly, the government still believes that it must act as the great white father not only to our Indians but also to groups like our veterans. The government says, "We know what is best for you; we have studied the question. We sit here in Ottawa and we know what is good for the people of this country." Our veterans are hard done by. Rising living costs make it hard for them to make ends meet, and so far there is no sign that veterans incomes are to be brought into line with living costs.
The fourth group I wish to speak about is made up of our Indian people. In this country we have not begun to help our Indians and Metis in an adequate way. The other day I was pleased to see on my desk a communication from the Metis of Alberta. I have not yet studied the justice of their position but I like the tone of their demands. These people are now saying, "We have listened long enough; now we want straight answers to straight questions." This session is drawing to an end and our Indians have not been dealt with
9952	COMMONS
The Budget-Mrs. Maclnnis justly. Many of them have incomes well below the poverty level.
The fifth group I shall speak of consists of immigrants. They come to this country and have many difficulties to face. Although many centres across Canada try to help our immigrants, they still need help. The Vancouver authorities try to help immigrants. The Vancouver School Board has been bombarding the government with requests for assistance with language training. The board wants the Department of Manpower and Immigration to help pay for English courses so that immigrants may be taught English and obtain jobs. English is not being taught, properly and adequately, to immigrants in Vancouver, the reason being that the Department of Manpower does not think it is under any obligation to provide English courses. I point out that unless immigrants have a knowledge of English, they will find it very difficult to obtain jobs in British Columbia.
The Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield) talked about the farmers, and I, too, wish to talk about the farmers. Many of our farmers face hard times, and this budget does not help them. My colleague the hon. member for Moose Jaw (Mr. Skoberg) is reported in a press article to have said yesterday that farmers without cash ought to be allowed to pay their income tax by dumping sacks of wheat, damp or dry, on Parliament hill. That would be payment in kind. The minister may think it inconvenient to be paid with grain but, as my colleague from Moose Jaw said, "There's just no bloody cash,... period." The government has done very little for our farmers.
Next I wish to talk about women. I have received a letter saying that 76 single working mothers in Toronto would like the government to allow them deductions for babysitting expenses. Without babysitters they cannot go out to work and support their families and they need deductions if they are to afford babysitters. I have been talking about this matter ever since I came here. If all the words of consideration the minister has uttered on this question were to be strung together they would stretch from Victoria, British Columbia, to St. John's, Newfoundland. So far, however, babysitting expenses are not deductible. This is another matter on which the minister ought to take action.
Next I shall talk about the poor and the poverty stricken people across this country. If we we are to believe the Economic Council, there are millions of poor in Canada. I was

DEBATES	June 10. 1969
much interested in the report of the Canadian Council of Churches and the Canadian Catholic Conference which studied the question of the Christian conscience and poverty. This Church group said in its report following the May, 1968, meeting in Montreal that the poor are no longer willing to accept the old attitudes. According to the report of the church group the deprived now say to the privileged, "Damn your charity; give us justice." This budget does not give our poor people justice.
I could go on talking about old age pensioners, the retired, our young people, veterans, Indians, immigrants, farmers, single mothers supporting families, the poor. The reaction of these people to this budget is one long, collective groan. They are groaning because their faith in this government has collapsed. Abraham Lincoln once said that the legitimate object of government is to do for a community of people what they need to have done but cannot do for themselves. Our government subscribes to this creed in wartime but not in peacetime. We must convince this government to subscribe to this creed in peacetime and to do for our people in peacetime what it has only done for them so far in wartime.
Members of my party have outlined what measures the government ought to enact. The Carter report ought to be implemented. After all, the taxpayers paid good money for that report which says that people should be taxed according to their ability to pay. We have told the government that it must protect Canadian industries from the encroachments of foreign corporations, no matter whether they hail from the United States, South Africa or elsewhere. We have said revenue must be used to assist the public sector. Money must be used for hospitals, housing, education, pensions and pollution and not to meet the debts of private companies which pile up a debt of $80 million that is promptly forgiven by the government on the ground that it is a technicality. We have said that the talk of a guaranteed income has to be made a reality. This patchwork of handouts and support involving various kinds of welfare must be supplanted by a good guaranteed income scheme which will protect people.
[DOT] (4:50 p.m.)
These are the needs the federal government should be looking after in 1969. These and the all-important need of getting genuine co-operation from people through local organizations are what are required. They are something
June 10, 1989	COMMONS
this government knows nothing about and could not care less about. Until the government reckons with societies of people in housing developments, with co-operative groups of people in the field of merchandising, with people who want to work together to build their own health clinics and who would be willing to support these co-operative local groups, any talk of participatory democracy is just so much wind.
These are the things the government should be doing instead of sitting here in Ottawa, backed up by the civil service and the economists, telling all the people that belt-tightening is good for the figure and it will not hurt very much if you think it won't. It is the belts of the people here in Ottawa that are not being tightened. We must have investment to care for the needs of people. That is the only way we are going to be able to build democracy as defined by the words of Abraham Lincoln, that is, government of the people, by the people and for the people.
We shall support the amendment of the official opposition and the amendment of the New Democratic party. We shall vote against this budget which falls short of meeting the important needs of the majority of the Canadian people.

subtopic: THE BUDGET
subsubtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in view of the continued inflationist pressures in this country, it has become necessary for the Canadian government to introduce a semi-annual budget instead of an annual budget and this principle is approved by economists, businessmen and financiers in Canada, because they find it necessary and timely to review the economic evolution of Canada more rapidly or quickly than before and to make, as needs are felt, adequate improvements.
It goes without saying that the announcement of a budget always brings about turmoil among people who are anxious to know the measures that the government intends to take and the exact economic situation as well.
Then there is a suspense which, of course, comes to an end on the evening of the budget speech and from that moment on, everyone makes his comments on the positions announced by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson). Financial critics from the opposition parties, economists, businessmen, financiers and all the taxpayers give their views.
The budget brought down on June 3 is a practical and a favourable one, since it does 29180-630
DEBATES	9953
The Budget-Mr. F. Leblanc not announce any tax increases and, moreover, is a balanced budget. Although some people might contemplate and, in fact, advocate other solutions, I can hardly disapprove the Minister of Finance. I wish to congratulate him for the magnificent job he has done since he is responsible for the finances of the country.
The plague of inflation is not peculiar to our country, since this phenomenon exists in every country of the world that enjoys intensive economic progress.
Inflation is a major problem that must be attacked directly to control it. Recently, I had the honour, with several hon. members, to participate in the 12th meeting of the Canada-U.S. Interparliamentary Association and this problem was discussed during the meetings of the trade and finance committee.
I found that the United States also use now conventional methods to control this problem, that is through fiscal and monetary measures necessary under the circumstances, and they have not yet succeeded in finding miraculous solutions. As in our case, they are reluctant to take the coercive measures advocated by several people. In this connection, I read recently, in the Hamilton Spectator, laudatory comments about the federal government, with regard to its anti-inflationary policy, and I quote:
Inflation is more than a simple problem. It is a continuous and destructive anxiety that weakens the purchasing power of the dollar, affects the prices of Canadian exports, creates with a new army of shame-faced poors among those who have only a fixed income, social clashes of all kinds.
According to many, such ill-effects caused by inflation are quite enough to justify drastic measures on the part of the government. More stringent measures may be considered in the future, when attempts to educate the public and promote voluntary restrictions have failed. But, at the present stage of Canadian economic development, the government shows wisdom in choosing, instead of a rigid system of wage and price control, a solution implying research and education. The government and its advisers still have a lot to learn about the complex economic forces that create inflation. And this applies equally to the world of business and to labour. Investigations of individual cases should give us a wealth of new knowledge.
Furthermore, it is in this spirit that the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Basford) has established the Prices and Incomes Commission. Our American colleagues were surprised to learn of the existence of such a Comission in our country, as they have not themselves gone as far as that in their efforts to control inflation. Obviously, insufficient control in the United States may greatly affect our country's position, because
9954	COMMONS
The Budget-Mr. F. Leblanc of the important economic relations between the two countries at the present time.
[DOT] (5:00 p.m.)
The inflationary spiral being stronger in the United States than in Canada, it is only normal that we should feel its effects constantly.
Our country cannot control inflation if our suppliers all over the world do not take really effective and appropriate measures. However, it is comforting to see our government performing some quite remarkable feats, such as a balanced budget in our present circumstances without increasing taxes in any way. In fact, we can say that taxation has reached the saturation point in our country, consider -
DEBATES	June 10, 1969
ing all the taxes raised by all governments, provincial, municipal and federal.
Mr. Speaker, it is strange to see that the taxpayers in the province of Quebec have experienced since 1960 an increase in their provincial taxes and a decrease in their federal taxes. Not long ago, Mr. Jean-Pierre Bonhomme, of the newspaper La Presse, published an article supplying comparative figures for 1960 and 1968, that was entitled Taxes payable by an individual residing in the province of Quebec in I960 and in 1968 and I quote:

The Minister of Finance has stated that there is another way to bring into play supply and demand to control inflation. It is to defer amortization or depreciation on commercial buildings erected from now on until the end of 1970. Such a plan was used 10 or 15 years ago and proved successful. All capital expenditures were then submitted to such a restriction which was later lifted after having achieved its aim. It is good to note that the present measure does not go as far as that since it does not apply to houses, industrial buildings, public services, public establishments, underpriviledged areas which are in fact protected by it since even if they do not represent inflationary factors they are subjected to it.
The Minister of Regional Economic Expansion (Mr. Marchand) stated on May 26, 1969 that the bill on grants to regional development would make it possible to provide some very strong incentives to industry, in order to increase employment in areas where it is low. Unemployment in certain areas is also an evil which must be eradicated as soon as possible, in order that Canadians throughout the country may satisfy their essential needs and fully identify themselves with Canadian life.
However, the incentives announced only apply to depressed areas and if we want to

increase investments in all areas of Canada, in order to meet an ever increasing demand by raising productivity, I will take the liberty of making a few suggestions to the Minister of Finances, since he intends to undertake a complete review of the Income Tax Act.
Among the necessary incentives to attract risk capital in operations which are vital to our economic development, I suggest in the first place that the 20 per cent exemption paid by Canadian companies be raised to 50 per cent. I also suggest to the province of Quebec to do likewise. This government could also increase tax exemptions for research costs. It could increase tax deductions to companies developing our natural resources, especially in the case of Canadian companies. In addition to subsidizing jobs in underdeveloped areas, the government could allow companies to deduct from their taxable income double the expenses incurred for the retraining and education of their employees. No doubt those measures could be intensified, and I trust the Minister of Finance is competent enough to examine the possibility of implementing those suggestions and many others, of which he surely thought with his imagination and creative mind. With the help of his department's technicians and experts he will certainly find the most adequate solutions for the economy of the whole country.
June 10, 1969

To relieve the father whose revenue is less than $5,000 a year, the minister could study for the future the possibility of lowering taxes but without putting the entire burden on the wage-earner who gets between $5,000 and $10,000. The father should get the exemption for education fees when a student is not earning money and cannot And a summer job.
The minister could also raise the statutory exemption with regard to charitable donations and medical expenses, from $100 to $200.
Mr. Speaker, it would be easy of course to stretch the list of suggestions. However, to give a chance to all those who wish to express their views, since the debate is limited to four days, I conclude by saying that I am proud to be a Canadian, to live in a country with such extraordinary resources and wealth, of unparalleled beauty and magnificence. I am happy to be a member of a government that can take its responsibilities and does all it can to create a just and prosperous society in Canada, based upon the private enterprise system, which is the source of the highest standards of living in the whole world.

subtopic: THE BUDGET
subsubtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to take part in this debate for two reasons, first to make some general comments with respect to the budget introduced by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) and, second, to say something about the effect of government action on the Canadian tobacco industry, particularly as it relates to the farmers, the people who grow and produce the tobacco.
[DOT] (5:10 p.m.)
In all sincerity I would like to commend the Minister of Finance, as many hon. members have already done, for producing a balanced budget. When deficits have occurred in public spending over a number of years it is always refreshing to find that at long last we are able to balance the budget. I suppose it is elementary to say that there are two ways in which this can be done. The first is by cutting down government expenditures to a level that makes the government live within its income, and the other way is to raise taxes to finance the expenditures already undertaken. Canadians across our land have been deeply disturbed that the government has been unable to regulate the problem and has been unable to set up guidelines for individuals for municipal governments in the various
June 10, 1969

The Budget-Mr. W. Knowles municipalities of Canada and for the provincial governments, guidelines which if properly laid down and observed by the senior government would be the most effective way, I think, in which to apply the brakes to runaway inflation.
Previous speakers in this debate have cited some glaring examples of wasteful spending by various departments of the government. Three examples come to mind which have been mentioned before. One of the most glaring is the runaway cost of the arts centre which skyrocketed from approximately $8 million to $46 million. Then there was the cost involved in refitting the Bonaventure. So vast a sum of money was poured into that ship that now she is known as the Waldorf of the waves. Surely she must be goldplated.
Another large expenditure which is of concern to a great many people is related to the increase in the Prime Minister's staff, the greatest increase in the history of our country. A parliamentary return of last December indicated that as of November 1, 1968, the Prime Minister' office alone had hired 34 people at a total salary of $406,085. As of November 1, 1965, the office was able to get along with only 21 people at a total salary of $197,492. That means that in three years the staff increased by at least two-thirds and the salary total doubled. This is only part of the picture. The Prime Minister has also been building up the office of the Privy Council. According to the estimates for the 1969-70 fiscal year it will jump from 209 people a year ago to 287 people for 1969-70. The salaries and wages of manpower in the Privy Council are estimated for 1969-70 at $2,599,000, up from $1,842,500 in the current fiscal year. At this rapid rate of growth it will not be long before there are more people working in the Prime Minister's office than in the whole city hall in Toronto. Already the salaries paid the 34 people working for the Prime Minister are more than double the salaries paid the 34 people sitting in the legislature and cabinet of the province of Prince Edward Island. If this trend continues the Prime Minister will soon have hired more people than he has kissed.
I believe the government should have greater concern-and this is a concern of all people-about the burgeoning bureaucracy and the failure of government departments to abide by some of the recommendations made by the Auditor General year after year and about which year after year nothing is done.
The second way budgets are balanced is by increasing taxes. This is something to which

we object. It is certainly the least palatable method. The minister has been able to forecast a considerable surplus to be juggled with, shall I say, in another year.
Perhaps I might be so bold as to make some suggestions concerning how he might use the surplus he has forecast in a manner that would bring relief to the Canadian people. First of all, it would seem to me that the basic exemption of $1,000 for individuals in respect of income tax should certainly be increased. It has remained at that figure since it was first instituted years ago. If at that time it represented living costs, surely now it should be increased two or three times. I believe that if this were done it might answer the complaint of the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway (Mrs. Maclnnis) in respect of people receiving the old age security pension being taxed on any amount over a $105 monthly payment. This could easily be remedied by increasing the basic exemption for income tax purposes to $2,000 or $3,000.
Surely the Minister of Finance could talk to the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Cote) and show him that it is most unfair that taxpayers who have children attending university should be allowed an exemption of only $500 each. This is insignificant; it is a pittance. It simply does not begin to represent the cost of sending a student to university. In the same regard I might mention the government's treatment of university students who try to earn income in the summer in order to provide for their education. They are forced to pay income tax. They are also forced to pay into the Canada Pension Plan. Why should they not be able to wait until they have completed their education and joined the working force before they have to make these payments? It seems rather strange that on the one hand the government takes this money away from them in the form of taxes and payments into the Canada Pension Plan and on the other hand offers them loans to finance their education.
I wish now to become more specific and draw to the attention of the Minister of Finance and all hon. members the economic importance to Canada of a particular industry, the tobacco industry especially as it involves the farmer producers of leaf tobacco. Tobacco growing is the one bright spot in the agricultural economy today. As has been mentioned by many hon. members, there is a problem in western Canada because the wheat producers simply do not have sufficient cash income with which to operate. The
June 10, 1969

agricultural economy is in difficulty but tobacco production is the one bright spot in the whole sad picture. However, if present attitudes and practices of the government are continued these producers will be faced with the same difficulty.
I believe it should be said that the tobacco crop is being grown on the light blow sand of southwestern Ontario which was formerly waste and drifting soil. Now it is the highest priced agricultural land in the country. The marriage of the flue-cured tobacco plant to the sandy soils of southwestern Ontario has had a salutary effect. Flue-cured tobacco for cigarettes was introduced in Canada about 1913 in Essex County in Ontario and by the mid-1930's had spread to 12 other counties. Today Canadian flue-cured tobacco is produced in wide areas of Ontario, Quebec and the maritime provinces of Nova Scotia, New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island. In 1967, Canada's second largest crop year, farmers produced over 214,702,000 pounds of flue-cured cigarette tobacco with a total value of $141,112,000 to farmers. Today 99 per cent of all tobacco used in Canada is grown in Canada by Canadian farmers. This is something we should not lose sight of. If today tobacco production were banned in Canada and all farmers stopped growing tobacco, tobacco simply would be imported from abroad and the manufacture and smoking of cigarettes would continue.
I think the agricultural segment of our society which produces tobacco should be recognized for its ability, investment, hard work and willingness to take a risk against the hazards of weather and so on to produce in Canada a product which we use in Canada. Over 51 million pounds of tobacco was exported in 1967 for a dollar return of $57 million. More will be said about this later.
The growers and producers of tobacco are regulated by the Ontario Flue-Cured Tobacco Growers Marketing Board Association which is organized under the Ontario Farm Products Marketing Act. There are 3,774 farmer members operating 4,262 farms for which there is allotted a basic quota of 152,416 acres. Besides these owner-growers in Ontario there are about 1,163 sharegrowers registered with the Tobacco Board. While Ontario growers produce about 95 per cent of Canada's flue crop, Quebec and the maritime provinces add about another 200 growers and some 7,000 acres of flue-cured tobacco to the Canadian industry.

The Budget-Mr. W. Knowles [DOT] (5:20 p.m.)
The latest reliable figures on capital investment on these farms, and I want hon. members to note that the survey was made in 1963 but subsequently updated, show that today there is a grand total of capital investment in Canada on tobacco farms of $435,696,000. That is a considerable amount of money invested in an industry in our country which is serving well the farming community. The assessment on tobacco farms ranges from two to three times greater than that on general farms with the same growth and same building conditions.
The sale of flue-cured tobacco in Canada amounts ordinarily to over $155 million per year. The return in 1968 was $152 million, down slightly, and in 1967 the figure was $135 million. During the 11-year period of auction sales through our exchanges, that is, from 1957 to 1967, tobacco sales totalled over $1 billion from Ontario, Quebec and the mari-times. This was money in the pockets of the farmers of this country. The largest share of these dollars found its way through production costs into the business life of the community, perhaps as much as 50 per cent in wages alone. Most of the balance, other than taxes, was funnelled into the local economy in the form of food, fuel, clothing, machinery and so on.
Let us consider the direct contribution this industry makes to the coffers of the federal government. I am sure the minister is very well aware of this, but I wish to state this for the benefit of hon. members who may not appreciate the importance of this industry to the economy of t'he country so far as excise tax and exports are concerned.
First of all, tobacco is one of Canada's top export commodities. In 1968 Canadian flue-cured tobacco exports to all countries amounted to about 55 million pounds, the largest share going to the United Kingdom, our second largest trading partner next to the United States. More than $51 million worth went to the United Kingdom. Tobacco is second only to wheat in the value of agricultural exports and brought, as I said, $57 million in earning export trade. This helped our trade balance. As already referred to twice by the hon. member for Halton (Mr. Whiting), one of the greatest needs in our economies is that we keep up our export trade and maintain a favourable trade balance.
Mr. Keith of Imperial Tobacco said in his report that the federal government received
9958	COMMONS
The Budget-Mr. W. Knowles over $555 million in excise taxes on tobacco. This is the easiest and most economic tax to collect. It was the fourth largest revenue earner for the federal government. More than $8 of every $100 spent by the federal government comes from the excise tax on tobacco. It is exceeded only by income tax, general sales tax and import duties. When we consider the taxes also levied by provincial governments in respect of tobacco, which total led some $85 million in 1967, this makes a grand total to federal and provincial governments of $723 million in tax revenue.
If this is important to our economy we should be taking some note of what another department of the government is endeavouring to do for tobacco growers. Having demonstrated this economic impact on the part of the tobacco growers, I think it is time the Minister of Finance took aside his colleague, the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Munro), and explained the economic facts of government.
We who grow tobacco crops feel that an overzealous and poorly documented attack has been made on the tobacco industry. The farmers who produce this crop feel they have been stigmatized by this unwarranted attack. We deny vigorously and forcefully that there has been any case made to so stigmatize the product we produce. By the very evangelical zeal and diversity of this attack on the industry it appears that the Department of National Health and Welfare hopes to compensate for the weakness of the attack it has carried forward.
We learned in the Standing Committee on Health, Welfare and Social Services that this case is based almost entirely on statistical evidence mainly gathered from the United States' Surgeon-General's report. Statistics only indicate trends or associations; they do not constitute proof. One should examine this statistical evidence and decide how it is gathered and how these statistics are interpreted.
We learned from a statistical expert how the Surgeon-General of the United States gathered these statistics which form the basis of this attack on our industry. This material was gathered by house to house canvassing. If the head of a household was not present a junior member of the family would supply the information. How in the world would he know what his grandfather died of or how many packs of cigarettes his father smoked? These are things that cast doubt on this zealous and unwarranted attack on our industry.

DEBATES	June 10, 1969
No experimental evidence has been introduced to show that there is a causal relationship between the smoking of cigarette tobacco and lung cancer or other respiratory diseases. Many experts testified before the committee, individual leaders in their fields. I could read from several of their statements but I will content myself by referring to what only two had to say.
Let me read from the statement presented by William B. Ober, a physician in New York city. He is a professor of pathology at the New York medical college and a director of laboratories at Knickerbocker Hospital. He had this to say:
I believe that the proposed legislation which this committee is considering had its formal inception in a speech given by the Hon. John Munro, your minister of health, given on December 19, 1968. I have read that speech, and it is a credit to Mr. Munro's desire to protect the health of his fellow Canadians.
Perhaps I might interject here. Those of us who are closely associated with the tobacco industry are just as concerned, but we do want to be shown. Dr. Ober continued:
Unfortunately some of his analogies are poorly chosen and I do think his aides have furnished him with data which fails to support his point of view.
Dr. Ober then gives an example of this type of information. He quotes the minister as follows:
I could ask every heavy smoker to try a 200 yard sprint at top speed, or a one mile run. Let them then come back, gasping and perhaps wheezing extensively, and tell me that their respiratory system has not been affected.
The statement of Dr. Ober then continues:
I submit that anyone who runs 200 yards at top speed, smoker or non-smoker, anyone who goes out for the mile run, smoker or non-smoker, will wind up at the finish line gasping for air. We have all seen photographs of non-smoking athletes in the pink of condition, taken as they breast the tape, and they all show faces contorted with air hunger. No. the reason runners gasp for air is not because they smoke. Bather it is because they are using up more oxygen than the normal gas exchange in the lungs can supply. In the physiology laboratory this is called oxygen debt. The Minister of Finance might apply the analogy to problems of currency flow and the question of international exchange-
[DOT] (5:30 p.m.)
We have other experts in other fields who cast very grave doubts on this unwarranted attack to which I have taken exception. John P. Wyatt, who is professor and chairman of the department of pathology at the University of Manitoba had this to say, and I will just
June 10, 1969

quote one sentence from his lengthy testimony:
In my opinion, there is insufficient evidence for attributing an established causal role in these conditions to cigarette smoking.
He is referring to the diseases of the respiratory tract.

speechtext:
I should like to draw the following story from the classics as it seems to illustrate the attitude of the officials of the Department of National Health and Welfare. We all know the story of Don Quixote who was forever tilting at windmills on the plains, thinking they were giants who were about to do him in. It seems to me that the officials of our Department of National Health and Welfare are rather like white knights mounted on chargers tilting at windmills, and the only windmills they see are cigarettes which, according to them, are the demons. Surely the task of the federal government and of the department ends when they have pointed out to all the Canadian people that there may be hazards in the smoking of cigarettes and tobacco. They have done this most amply. We feel that it is unnecessary for them to pursue with such evangelical fervour this vicious attack against our tobacco industry.
May I say in conclusion that tobacco growers are pleased to note that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) did not levy additional taxes on the tobacco industry. We who grow the tobacco and who are involved in this industry, feel that the point has been reached at which the law of diminishing returns begins to act. The minister cannot tax further without decreasing the use of the product and the net national returns to the government. In view of the weaknesses of the case of the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Munro) we ask him to get off the backs of the tobacco growers, the farmers who produce in this country, and to concentrate on the more
The Budget-Mr. Beaudoin obvious health hazards which affect the people of our country.

subtopic: THE BUDGET
subsubtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I feel most happy to have the opportunity to comment the speech delivered by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson), and before getting to the heart of the matter, I would hate not to commend my leader for his speech of yesterday.
I think that he dealt with all the important points of the budget or the mini-budget presented to us. While I support my leader, I would like nevertheless to point out a few predominant facts of the budget speech made by the Minister of Finance, of which many are unacceptable to me.
I fully agree that we must fight inflation, but I reject the means put forward to that end by the government. In my opinion, those changes are again made at the expense of the poor, particularly those who can hardly earn their living in Canada. For some time now we have been receiving requests from farmers who are complaining about lower government subsidies for their dairy products.
Is it that the Minister of Finance had already given his orders before bringing down his budget?
I was told that this was due to the new dairy policy which is aimed at encouraging dairy exports especially of manufactured products.
It is obvious that the present Liberal government has failed in this field, as it did in respect of wheat.
I see that the government wants to ruin the farmers and all the working classes in Canada. It gives with one hand and takes with the other, using the means already applied to help the people and fight inflation.
As for unemployment, the Minister of Finance is advocating an incentive program for industry. Does he mean that the government will grant further subsidies to the industries? I believe we will have to establish in this field strict control over the use made of our money-I mean the taxpayer's money collected by way of taxes-so that the situation which arose in the case of Canadian Vickers will not occur every year.
This company received subsidies adding up to several million dollars, but to what avail? It is going out of business. What did they do with the government money or rather, to be fair, with the taxpayers' money? Is it the intention of the government to carry on this
June 10, 1969

The Budget-Mr. Beaudoin way? I would like to quote in this respect, the very words of the Minister of Labour (Mr. Mackasey) who said a month ago and I quote: Canadian Vickers received from the government millions of dollars in subsidies and it should have acted differently.
As far as the $100 exemption on goods-I mean the tariff exemption-granted to Canadian citizens back from a visit to the United States, I wonder whether this is really intended to promote the sale of Canadian products? Many people resort to trickery when they go to the United States for 48 hours. I am familiar with this because I live very close to the United States border. Why buy Canadian products which sell for more than $100 when you can get them for $100 in the United States without paying duty?
The prices of Canadian products might go down, but how many companies will close down, thus adding to the unemployment due to the lay-off of many workers?
And then we will have more unemployment. It is a vicious circle, a double-edged weapon, in short a problem which this government seems unable to solve. That is why I give my complete support to the amendment of the hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert) which reads as follows:
That all the words after "house" be struck out and the following substituted therefor:
"regrets the continuing inability of the government to curb the relentless increase in the cost of living since 1965, while increasing the hardship of the unemployed, the poor, pensioners, farmers and other victims of the just society."
Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Finance boasts about achieving the first real surplus since 1955-57, when the Right Hon. Louis St. Laurent was then Prime Minister of Canada. What a discovery, what a victory, and at what price.
On May 22, 1969, speaking on the motion introduced by the Ralliement ereditiste to provide the country with a policy of distribution of goods and services which would enable every citizen to get his share of the Canadian wealth, the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion (Mr. Marchand) admitting his inability to do so, said in a somewhat sarcastic tone, and I quote:
[DOT] (5:40 p.m.)
I have not found the philosopher's stone nor any magic formula: I have no direct communication with the Holy Ghost.
Such nice sentences with a religious ring. But they show a total inability to deal with some problems.
According to this minister, it is impossible to fight inflation because inflation is of a 
regional nature, and if the intent is to change our present tax system, this would benefit the Maritimes while creating inflation in Ontario and elsewhere.
Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Finance is simply applying discriminatory measures against Ontario, British Columbia and Alberta, two of those provinces having Social Credit governments.
Is it because everything is all right in those provinces? We wonder.
Therefore, at this stage, I want to refer to page 9419 of Hansard, and I quote:
I therefore propose that depreciation, or capital cost allowances, for tax purposes should be deferred for a period of two years on commercial buildings put in place up to the end of 1970. This would not apply to any form of housing, industrial building, utilities, or public institutions.
But this limitation or exemption will apply to cities with a population over 50,000. We have here an obvious contradiction between what the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion (Mr. Marchand) said on May 22, and the statement made on June 3 by the Minister of Finance.
At that time, the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion stated that he was unable to find a policy to deal with inflation in some regions without impoverishing other regions. But the Minister of Finance says that he has found one. Actually, he is applying different taxation formulas, according to the regions.
I ask, if it is possible to act that way, why does the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) not apply different monetary policies in various parts of the country?
Why does he not allow the Bank of Canada to relax credit to encourage regional development in Quebec and the Maritimes? Why not have Bank of Canada branch offices at the provincial level?
When he brought down his mini-budget on June 3, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) said, as reported on page 9413 of Hansard:
From the review which I shall give tonight,
I think it will be evident that we are well launched upon this course.
Talk about launching! Ask the taxpayers, ask the farmers, and all classes of society, several of which are living in poverty, ask them if they like that launching?
The minister speaks of our being well launched on this course. He forgets to say that though the launching was good, many repairs were needed, and the motor of our economy stalled completely many times since October 16 when the first budget was brought
June 10, 1969	COMMONS
down and June 3 when the second one was introduced.
Indeed, while levying a special basic tax of
2	per cent, the minister is forced to keep the
3	per cent surcharge which we had been promised would be abolished, as the minister himself said on June 3, as reported on page 9417 of Hansard, and I quote:
I am not proposing any increase in either personal or corporate tax rates beyond their current levels nor an increase in sales tax, but I am proposing tonight that the personal income tax surtax of 3 per cent on "basic tax" in excess of $200 and the corporation income surtax applicable for the years 1968 and 1969 should be extended until December 31, 1970.
That is quite a find! The minister confirms that there were delays because he has been forced to extend measures that will increase taxes by $155 million in 1970.
Mr. Speaker, here is what the present government proposes in two, three or perhaps four words: Look for truth in the dark.
The Minister of Regional Economic Expansion is reported in Hansard for May 22, at page 8951, as having said:
As for us, we are humans looking for truth in the darkness.
The budget speech delivered on June 3 proves it beyond doubt. It is obvious that this government is looking for truth in the dark, and that, like the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion (Mr. Marchand), it is in complete darkness. No wonder they bring in gloomy and confused budgets. As the ministers walk in the dark, they are bound to have gloomy ideas.
The least we can suggest to the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion and the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson), is to find a candle, a lantern, a flashlight or at least a little 40-watt light.
It is obvious that the Minister of Finance, like the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion, "is looking for truth in the dark." What is he doing? He is feeling his way; he steps forward, he steps back, he hesitates. He imposes on the poor a social development tax.
Since when has tax been a sign of development? On the contrary, it is a set-back, since it reduces the purchasing power of consumers. Clearly, this social development tax is a result of his groping in the dark.
By maintaining the 3 per cent tax, after having promised to abolish it, he takes a step forward or rather a step backwards, I think, in the dark always.
DEBATES	9961
The Budget-Mr. Beaudoin Certain tariffs which should not have been abolished until January 1972 are abolished so that industry will be in a better position to meet competition. I quote the words of the minister as reported in Hansard, page 9417:
To be specific: I propose that the final rates which were to come into effect on January 1, 1972, should come into effect as of tomorrow morning. This means that the remaining Kennedy Round tariff reductions which had not yet been given effect are to apply immediately.
And further on:
I recognize that some producers will feel they are being denied the time for adjustment to increased competition, which the phasing of the Kennedy Round reductions would have provided. However, I believe that in today's climate, when failure to counter inflation holds its own risks for our competitive position, more time is not necessary for our producers to adapt themselves to these tariffs.
Of course, when one administers in the dark,-as I just said,-one makes a decision at night, and the next morning, it is in effect. The minister said:
-more time is not necessary for our producers to adapt themselves to these tariffs.
Everything about the financial operations of a business must be changed overnight.
The minister also says: You must adapt to foreign competition! Lower your costs, lower your prices, because foreign products which will enter Canada more easily will strongly compete with yours and take hold of your market. That is the minister's way of thinking, or that of his colleagues who made such a suggestion.
At a time when Canada, particularly the province of Quebec, and including the eastern provinces, has a tremendous number of unemployed, I think that such policies are quite ill-timed.
How can Canadian producers lower their prices? By lowering the wages of the workers? Perhaps!
The Minister of Finance must have forgotten to consult his colleague the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion, former president of the Confederation of National Trade Unions, to be speaking like this.
Is it any wonder since the ministers are so much in the dark that they do not even see each other.
On June 3 1969, the Minister of Finance, while introducing his minibudget, also proposed, as recorded on page 9413 of Hansard, that the house approve the general budgetary policy of the government. Useless to say that the Ralliement creditiste is unable to endorse such a proposal, because we com-
June 10, 1969

The Budget-Mr. Beaudoin pletely disagree with the government and the Minister of Finance on their general budgetary policy.
To meet the increasing cost of living, which affects particularly small taxpayers, the Ral-liement creditiste expected the government, if it purported to run the country in the best interests of the people, to announce a reduction of the personal and corporate income tax, the curtailment of the 11 per cent tax on building materials, the definite removal of the 3 per cent surtax which was promised, fiscal reductions in order to promote economic development and measures to reduce interest rates.
[DOT] (5:50 p.m.)
On the contrary, we are advised that the application of the 3 per cent surtax will be extended, that the 11 per cent tax on building materials will be maintained, that the capital cost allowances on commercial buildings put in place up to the end of 1970 in Ontario, British Columbia and Alberta will be deferred for two years and that tariff amendments which are going to hurt our industries and increase unemployment will be put through.
Mr. Speaker, how can we fight inflation if the government does not take the necessary means to lower the disastrous interest rates which push prices up daily and only succeed in making trust compagnies wealthy at the expense of small borrowers?
The profits of banks increase daily. Indeed, during the first six months of 1969, according to the banks' official reports the Imperial Bank of Commerce has realized a net profit of 34.5 per cent in 6 months and the Royal Bank of Canada, 14.1 per cent.
Mr. Speaker, I think that this is good business.
The Canadian National Bank has realized a profit of 7.5 per cent, the Bank of Nova Scotia, of about $8 million, the Bank of Montreal, of 63 cents per share against 27 cents in 1968, and the Provincial Bank made a profit of 29.1 per cent.
We thus clearly realize that the money spent by the government, by the departments, the money created by the Bank of Canada and handed over to the departments by the Bank of Canada, is loaned to the government, and is reimbursed afterwards through direct taxation on personal and corporate incomes.
Now that it is recognized that not a single dollar bill in circulation, not one credit dollar has not been put in circulation by a bank through a bank loan which must be reim-
bursed, it is obvious that all the money in circulation, even taxes, belongs to the banks, and must ultimately return to them.
Mr. Speaker, it is impossible, no matter how hard the government and the Minister of Finance may try, to balance a budget under such circumstances, unless one assumes that the purchasing poser which remains in the hands of the taxpayers is but the balance of bank loans not yet recalled, namely a debt to the banking system or the export surpluses.
It is therefore obvious that a balanced budget, in such conditions, can only recognize that all national wealth belongs to the banking system which has complete control over the flux of the economic body in the present conditions.
As long as the government is unable to get free from the hold of the banking system, how will it be possible to administer? As long as it is obliged to go and borrow from someone more powerful than it is, how will it be possible to help the poor in spite of all the ways the minister and his colleagues would think of using? The government will remain in the dark if it is forced to do business with short-sighted people whose eyes are closed and whose doors are shut.
But to get out of that darkness, to escape that misery, the government should consider the proposals of the Ralliement creditiste concerning the use of the Bank of Canada, as a tool at the service of Canadians. Then, it will be able to provide an enlightened administration, and the ministers-the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion included-will have found truth in the light and not in the dark.

subtopic: THE BUDGET
subsubtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to commence by saying that I am entitling this budget the "Ben Benson budget bounce". Like a rubber ball, infla-minister's rosy statements, the budget offers tion keeps coming back. In spite of the little to the ordinary Canadian except a continuation of high taxes, with no hope of relief in the near future. The average Canadian wage earner is compelled to pay over $20 a week in taxes at the present time. This is unwarranted filching by this government from the taxpayer's pocket. Canadians are entitled to tax relief. They would have welcomed tax relief across this country, as it would have enabled them to plan for the future.
June 10. 1969	COMMONS
Not only has no tax relief been provided, but the 3 per cent surtax has been continued with no shadow of justification. I warn the minister that if the present unjustifiably high rate of taxation continues much longer he will be faced by a tax revolt in this country. Time and again this government has promised tax reform. Where is tax reform in this budget? This budget is just a continuation of the same repressive taxation which we have had for the past two years. What has happened to the reforms recommended in the Carter commission report? They have been shoved to one side. This government must be taken to task for following a repressive policy of high taxation, high costs, high inflation and high interest rates. There has been no change in any of these fields.
The minister put on a shocking display of bad taste on television when he dared to suggest he was following a policy which would aid the ordinary Canadian. In this respect he was ascribing to Canadians across this land a degree of gullibility equal only to his own. The budget is a continuation of policies which have placed on the people of this country the most oppressive taxation and inflation burden that they have ever been asked to carry, with the possible exception of the war years.
There is no relief in this budget for the western farmer. There is nothing for the small businessman, and nothing for the consumer, the housewife, plagued by constantly rising food costs about which the department of consumer affairs has proved powerless to do anything. There is not one five cent piece of relief for the Canadian wishing to buy a home or the Canadian who already owns a home. There is no relief from the unnecessary tax on building materials, or from any of the other taxes which plague the householder and homeowner.
On top of this, the government imposes a further nuisance tax, a tax on air travel. This is simply another means of getting into the taxpayer's pocket. The government has done nothing about dealing with the high price of farm implements or curbing interest rates. The time has come for the government to offer interest free loans to farmers, but nothing has been done in this regard. Surely, with the armies of economists that the government has at its disposal it would have been possible to come up with a more constructive measure than a nuisance tax on air travel. Surely the government, in view of the difficulties in which the western Canadian farmer finds himself, could have come up with an interest free loan for the purchase of farm equipment.
DEBATES	9963
The Budget-Mr. Paproski
There is nothing in this budget to encourage exploration for oil and no sign of a national oil policy. It is a budget which neglects the necessary and devotes itself to the trivial and the obstructive. This budget will not encourage prosperity. As far as the individual is concerned, it will obstruct it.
Perhaps the most objectionable feature of the entire fiscal performance is the obvious disregard and neglect of western Canada. The deferment of capital cost allowances on construction in the western provinces is a slap in the face to western Canada. It is a deliberate penalizing of western Canadian prosperity. It is economic discrimination in its worst form. The minister proudly, and I think foolishly, hailed a budget surplus of some $250 million. Where is this money coming from? Is he going to extract it from western Canada? Is western Canada's economy once again to be sacrificed to eastern interests? This is the most iniquitous measure in a fatuous and feeble budgetary performance. If its purpose is to curb inflation, why is Montreal exempted? Why is the minister showing economic favouritism in his budget? Once again, this government is placing a premium on non-performance.
In light of this it would seem that the Liberal party has simply written off western Canada as a source of electoral support and is now going to penalize the western provinces, or attempt to force them into line. You cannot justify a tax policy that penalizes one part of the country and benefits the other parts. For too long western Canada has been contributing more than it has received. For too long we in the west have been made the victims of an unrealistic oil policy which permits foreign oil to be sold and distributed in Montreal while oil from western Canada is kept out. The time has come for the government to finance an all Canadian oil pipe line from Alberta to eastern Canada in order that we have access to eastern Canadian markets.
The latest discrimination embodied in the deferment of depreciation allowances on capital construction costs in the western provinces will do further damage to the economy of western Canada. In light of this, one wonders where the minister expects to raise his projected $250 million surplus. Does he expect revenues to continue at last year's level in spite of the failure to sell our wheat? Is the minister aware of the fact that at the end of May over 398 million bushels of wheat remained on hand? Unless the government can do something to rectify the mismanagement of wheat sales, we will face a serious
June 10. 1969

The Budget-Mr. Paproski
drop in national revenues in the coming fiscal year.
May I call it six o'clock?

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am asking the minister whether his projected revenues for the coming year take into account wheat sales at last year's level or at a level below last year's, as is the case at the present time. It would be interesting to know in this connection what projected sales are and what steps the government intends to take in order to avoid the largest surplus of wheat in our history. I suggest to the government that it should get on its feet and get out to where the boys grow wheat.
The government has been accused of taxing the rich to help the poor. I am happy to refute that charge. There is no evidence whatsoever that this government taxes the rich. What this government is doing is this: it is taxing the poor to help the rich. About two years ago this government took action to create a fiscal climate in which the rich could get richer while the poor got poorer. The government allowed bank interest rates to almost double. It has increased mortgage interest rates, imposed a succession duty that falls heavily on those with moderate incomes and allowed the housing industry to become the promoter's preserve while permitting homes to be priced out of the reach of all but the wealthy. This government has consistently favoured the larger financial institutions or interests in this country.
I ask, Mr. Speaker, who benefits from high interest rates? Is it the western farmer? Is it the city dweller who must secure a mortgage in order to provide a home for himself and his children? Is it the housewife who must pay inflated prices for bread I submit that the institutions which benefit most from high interest rates are the financial institutions. I ask the minister whether he is aware that banks in this country and kindred lending institutions recorded their highest profits in many years as a result of last year's increase in interest rates. The Minister of Finance


must be aware of these things; yet during an appearance on television he said that he was doing everything he could for the little people. We have high taxes, high interest rates inflated prices and a tax on homes. All these things the minister has preserved for the little people of Canada, for the farmers, workers and moderate wage earners. I say to the minister, come off it. Canadians are aware that no government has done more to reduce average incomes than has this government. In addition to a tax on the worker's pay cheque the government levies an insidious, indirect tax in the form of inflation. Finally, after death, it levies succession duties at rates higher than any we have known before.
