speechtext:
It is my hope that the provisions of this budget will undergo careful and critical examination in this chamber and that we, as Members of Parliament representing the public, will make it known to Canadians that we are opposed to a policy of high taxes, high interest rates and high prices. If one wishes to see a glaring example of irresponsibility on the part of the government one should look at taxes. After having imposed for two years the highest peacetime taxes in our history, the government offers no relief whatever to the hard pressed Canadian taxpayer. On behalf of the many Canadians across this country who feel they are entitled to tax relief at this time, Mr. Speaker, I object.
This evening, Mr. Speaker, we shall be voting on the subamendment moved by the hon. member for Waterloo (Mr. Saltsman) on behalf of the New Democratic Party. The subamendment regrets the failure of the government to grant relief from income tax to single persons with incomes below $2,000 a year and married persons with incomes below $4,000 a year. I have no difficulty in voting in favour of this subamendment. To me it means that we wish to see some relief given to people in these very low income brackets. They are the people who are hardest hit by the increase in the cost of living. Living costs have been going up for four years under this government. Of course, that does not mean that we wish to strike all such people off the tax rolls. Nor would I allow exemptions of $2,000 and $4,000 to those in all other tax brackets. The wording of the subamendment is vague, perhaps.
Furthermore, Mr. Speaker, I think the long term attack on poverty is going to involve a
June 10. 1969

rationalization of the social welfare system and the application of a concept such as a negative income tax which was discussed by my party during the last election campaign. In the meantime, we must consider the principle contained in the subamendment now before the house, namely, that some relief should be given to those in the lowest income groups who suffer most from inflation. We endorse that principle and will therefore vote in favour of the submendment.

subtopic: THE BUDGET
subsubtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, after hearing several members of the opposition say that the budget did not contain anything and would not solve anything, and after hearing the same members join to criticize the contents of this same budget, I feel compelled to take part in this debate.
I have noted particularly a few remarks of some members about the capital cost allowances for tax purposes, especially on commercial buildings, which are being deferred for a two year period.
I have noted the comments of the members for Waterloo and Edmonton West (Messrs. Saltsman and Lambert) and even those of the previous speaker to the effect that the deferred depreciation was discriminatory; indeed, that it would penalize some regions for their success.
The main aspect of this measure which consists in deferring for a temporary period only those tax incentives, especially in the areas mentioned, in order to stabilize prices, ensure a fair competition and direct capital towards housing, seems to have escaped them completely.
The member for Temiscamingue (Mr. Caouette) mentioned the Creditiste administrations of 33 and 18 years in two provincial governments in order to prove the theory he was putting forth. He seemed to imply that we should adopt the Creditiste theory as the only possible solution but he forgot to say that those two governments do not apply the theory which the member for Temiscamingue has been preaching for so long, but rather the monetary policy followed by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) in preparing the budget which he tabled in the house.
The hon. member has also omitted to say that the only province which experimented the system for 17 years, has only succeeded in driving away both residents and investments.
The Budget-Mr. Trudel It will take a long time before the damage caused by the Creditiste theory is repaired.
What the hon. members have failed to say is that Canadians are now spending more and more for leisure and services. About two years ago, 75 per cent of the money available was spent on durable goods. Now, the new trend is putting pressure on inflation at the present rate of change, because in 1970, 50 per cent of the personal income will be spent on leisure and no longer on durable goods or services.
It is the main reason for the changes proposed in the budget. The members have also forgotten that when he was preparing his budget, the minister really intended to fight inflation which he defines as a surplus of money, as compared to goods and to available services, which varies in certain sectors of economy and even in some areas of the country. They have also forgotten a few facts that I want to mention.
There was a $390 million surplus before the estimates, as compared to a previous deficit of $566 million. This represents a transfer of $1 billion in the economic impact at the federal level.
They have also forgotten that the government was able, during this period of price escalation, to maintain its expenditures at the same level for one year.
The minister was also able to increase grants to municipalities and provinces by $55 million in order to improve their financial position.
One other point they were careful not to mention is that this budget makes it possible to distribute 65 per cent of all taxes levied in Canada among the provinces and the municipalities. This percentage has been increasing steadily for several years.
The Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) has made available to the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce enough capital to raise exports to over $13 billion, making possible a trade balance for of $1,300 million in favour of Canada.
The Export Credit Insurance Corporation has ensured $246 million worth of goods in 1968, thus creating jobs for Canadians, mostly for Quebecers.
This budget, although very satisfactory, and even though our exports have increased by 19 per cent last year, is designed nevertheless to increase the output of finished products by our Canadian workers while decreasing the proportion of raw materials exported

June 10, 1969
The Budget-Mr. Trudel without local processing. This task has been entrusted to the Department of Regional Economic Expansion, who has already started on its work.
As I said at the beginning of my remarks, the capital cost allowances seem to have frightened some members. But it must be held in mind that in the three provinces involved, the number of commercial buildings has increased by 32.6, 31.6 and 9.3 per cent respectively, while in Quebec there was an expected of 6 per cent for the same period and the Canadian average, also for that period, showed an increase of 20 per cent. Moreover, this over-activity in commerical construction has led to wage demands, of $1.50 and even $2.00 an hour more than in the other areas of Canada, without meeting for all that the total requirements of those areas and the contractors.
A direct result will be to alleviate the pressure on capital used for the construction of commercial buildings and to ease the demand for housing, thus reducing the inflationary pressures, even in British Columbia, Alberta and Ontario.
For the other provinces, like Quebec, this measure will help to attract the industries needed to absorb the ever-increasing manpower coming on the labour market. There is no such increase elsewhere in the industrial field. In that province, more than 80,000 new jobs will have to be created yearly for five years.
This budget provides for the writing-off of the $125 million deficit for Expo, that is the federal share of the deficit.
Hon. members will recall also the extension of the provincial and municipal shares.
Canadians travelling abroad will enjoy additional exemptions.
Moreover, none of the opposition members who spoke mentioned manpower retraining, especially in Quebec and in the Maritimes.
We could give a long list of agreements for assistance to the provinces, involving expenditures of several million dollars yearly, made possible by this budget.
The federal-provincial conference is to be held this week in Ottawa, and I certainly must mention it briefly. If one takes into account that, at the present time, 50 per cent of the federal budget is earmarked for welfare allowances, and that the province of Quebec devotes 68 per cent of its budget to two items only, namely welfare and education, this meeting must consider not only tax 
sharing but also how that money is spent, at the three levels of government.
Out of a $3 billion budget, Quebec spends only $20 million to promote industry and trade, while the federal budget provides that 14.3 per cent of its total will be devoted to economic expansion directly benefiting that province and municipalities that need it most.
The department has more particularly considered the case of Quebec, as far as the building industry is concerned, and at present there is in that province a surplus of skilled labour. The minister has recognized this fact, and has relieved this anomaly by taking the above mentioned measures.
I have seen fit to take part in this debate to mention a few points that the hon. members on my left had completely ignored.
Therefore, I should like to close my remarks by congratulating the Minister of Finance for the planning he has effected in order to get a just society, by bridging the gap of the regional disparities, by making available to the other departments fiscal resources, to improve the lot of the people across Canada whether they are Frenchspeaking or English-speaking or to improve employment opportunities through the regional development program.
Moreover, he is allowing Canadians to secure the type of housing of their choice, and to express themselves in any of the two official languages of the country.
[DOT] (8:20 p.m.)

subtopic: THE BUDGET
subsubtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I could not help but be amused at the rather mystical and psychic comment flashed at us by our affable Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson), and which is contained in 'his white paper, that "since 1965 increases in prices have been larger than desirable, and public policy has been designed to replace inflationary expansion by balanced and sustained growth." Sometimes, Mr. Speaker, we wonder. We wonder also at the admissions, such as the one in his budget speech that "persistence of strong inflationary tides necessitates a re-assessment of our position." How long must we hear these things?
It was three years ago that the Liberal government was first warned that inflation had got out of 'hand. I happened to be one of those who warned them, as recorded at page 5609 of Hansard for May 27, 1966. I do not
June 10, 1969	COMMONS
like quoting my own speeches but this is positively what the record shows:
Mr. Chairman, I regret to intrude on your busy schedule but I think at this time, when we are on interim supply, I should raise this question which is of general interest to the nation. I think the lot of the consumer should be brought to the attention of the house and the committee.
First of all, Mr. Chairman, each of us in this country is a consumer. Present day government policy and the consequent high cost of consumer goods is storming the last bastion of individual hope and the individual right to live within one's means. It is now practically impossible for the head of a family, father or mother, individual or married couple, to make their modest salaries support their families from one pay day to the next.
Prices have skyrocketed all along the line in food, rent, clothing, fuel, transportation, medical bills, insurance, taxes and capital cost of housing both new and used. In this rapid and cruel escalation of costs this government has been a steady partner. Even its policies glaringly point to that fact. It is readily apparent that its policies support the super corporations which profit from and control our buyers' and consumers' economy.
The above conditions are now, three years latter, more pronounced, more acute, more rampant, and practically uncontrolled. But we still hear platitudes about re-assessments.
Since the 1962-63 fiscal year federal government spending is up over $6 billion, and up over $5 billion in the four years of "concerned anti-inflationary policy." Even now, Mr. Speaker, the Canadian Tax Foundation is predicting a 9.8 per cent rise in federal government spending this year-up from last year's increase. And when the Minister of Finance 'himself, having taken most of a white paper and a budget speech to assure us how aware and concerned the government is about inflation, and how excellent this budget is as an anti-inflationary weapon, then proceeds baldly to predict no fall in the rate of price increase in the coming year, we must wonder.
What has the Liberal government been doing these last four years? Nothing that would help the situation. We have had many tax increases during the past few years, and all of these in the name of fighting inflation. But a taxpayer wonders when he sees an 85 per cent increase in federal government spending since 1962-63, while the take from the personal income tax in that time has been boosted to 164 per cent of its 1962-63. level. And this year we know that Canadians will pay more in personal income taxes. This vicious spiral must be stopped. We have had four years of so-called anti-inflationary policy, four years of tax increases, and still we hear
DEBATES	9967
The Budget-Mr. Alkenbrack the Minister of Finance predicting no fall in the rate of price increase.
The Minister of Finance depends on inflation to balance this budget. A great share of the 32 per cent increase in personal income tax take is directly caused by inflation. Wages and salaries would not be going up so fast if we did not have inflation which seriously reduces the spending power of a man's income.
When consumer prices are going up by 4.7 per cent a year, a man has to make at least that much more to keep up. In fact, he has to make more. He does not enjoy an adjustment of his exemptions to allow for inflation. He just pays. If a family of four with an income of $5,000 received a 4.7 per cent increase, just enough to match the increase in the consumer price index, they would be penalized with a $49 tax increase. Their real income is no higher, but nevertheless they pay. And as a result we have been promised a balanced budget-perhaps

we hope.
The Minister of Finance, in his usual efficient fashion, has informed us that he expects a surplus of $250 million. How much of this is generated by the effect of inflation on tax revenues? We know that $275 million, which is $25 million more than his predicted surplus, comes from a once and for all speed up of corporate tax collections. That is fine for this year, but what will he do next year?
We know that the minister has saved over $200 million because some provinces have thus far stayed out of medicare. This allows him some flexibility for supplementary estimates, but should he really be allowed to crow that estimated 1969-70 spending has been reduced $20 million from last October's estimate, particularly when we remember that on February 4 his colleague tabled estimates totalling $11,858 million? We have seen too much of this playing around with the finances of the provinces. According to the minister's admission in the white paper the provinces moved from a $125 million deficit in 1967 to a $300 million surplus in 1968. He has, therefore, shown us who has taken on the responsibility in this fight against inflation, and it certainly is not the federal government. It is time the federal government became a leader against inflation instead of a beneficiary of inflation.
What has the government done? Expenditures have not been cut. In fact, they appear to be heading for a 9.8 per cent increase, and this up from last year's increase. The 3 per cent surcharge on personal and corporate
June 10, 1969

The Budget-Mr. Alkenbrack income has been maintained. Incidentally, the minister previously guaranteed this would not happen. They have added a tax on air travel. On this point, I wonder is it the minister's intention to extend such a tax to users of aircraft for work in the development of resources, especially in northern areas. If so, could he tell us what impact this is likely to have on such survey and development work?
The minister made a large noise about his daring new selective fiscal policy which resulted in a two-year deferral of capital cost allowances for commercial construction in urban centres of Ontario, Alberta and British Columbia. Mr. Speaker, we support the principle of selectivity. It is something our party called for years ago. But I am somewhat disappointed at the minister's refusal to get his feet wet. The minister seems to be testing the water with his big toe. Commercial construction represents only 8 per cent of all construction in Canada, and only about 5 per cent of all capital spending.
[DOT] (8:30 p.m.)
When we scale down this provision to the 22 cities involved we begin to talk of less than 4 per cent of capital spending. Even then there is good reason to doubt the impact of this move. The reason is so far advanced this year that we could not expect any impact so soon. On top of this, construction wage increases averaging 11.2 per cent last year- up from 9.1 per cent the year before-and escalating material costs make the cost of waiting much greater than the tax loss incurred by building now. Unfortunately, since the demand for buildings is so strong this move will quite likely result in rising rents, thus contributing to the inflation it seeks to cure.
The minister also attempted to convince the house that the Kennedy round tariff cuts would help hold the line on prices. We fully support in principle the Kennedy round agreements, and Canada can do well generally under the negotiated changes. But the Kennedy round was aimed at general tariff reduction in the interest of promoting trade and the more efficient allocation of activity internationally. It was not designed to combat inflation. Are the areas covered by the Kennedy round tariffs the most inflation sensitive? Are the specific cuts negotiated exactly what is required to control inflation? Administrative ease does not necessarily imply effectiveness. If tariffs were thought to be major contributors to inflation, why were cuts so limited and confined to the Kennedy round?

There are dangers here. The minister's argument that the lack of application for transitional assistance as a result of past reductions implies that this situation will continue, is logically week. Naturally, the severest impact will come from the final cuts after the dead wood has been cut away. We are not as confident as the minister about the regional effects involved. I would ask the minister in charge of regional development not to allow his efforts to be eroded before he gets going, and to intercede if cases of hardship in the slow growth areas should come to light.
The Kennedy round cuts were designed to meet a long-run problem. Their use as a short-run tool is questionable and experimentally speculative. We regret the failure of the minister to conclude an agreement with the United States for a similar speed-up. Tariffs are not always the factor causing Canadian prices to rise above U.S. prices. Need I remind the minister that quite often Canadian produced cars sell cheaper in the United States than in Canada? Tariffs are not to blame, and $80 million subsidies will not help.
I regret this government's tendency to act unilaterally and in bad faith in reneging on its agreements. This would be tempered somewhat if I expected that the Canadian consumer would receive the benefits of these cuts. We will be reminding the Minister of Consumer Affairs of his responsibility to see that they do. But the real tragedy, Mr. Speaker, is the many holes in this budget, the errors of omission. The minister continue to refuse to listen to our pleas for the abandonment of the social development tax. The minister ignores completely the high and rising interest rates which our consumers must face. Not once does he express concern that such rates are making a house an elusive dream for so many Canadians.
There is no concern at all for the terrible problems of poverty we find in Canada. I have them in my riding; we have our share. There is no concern, for example, for the old age pensioners whose only income is the pension on which they pay income tax. There is no advancement in the fight against regional disparity. Eastern and western farmers are ignored. We fear the continued impact of general tax policies on unemployment in the slow growth areas. Finally, the minister admits he expects no decline in the rate of price increase in the next year. This government has failed, Mr. Speaker, and the minister ought to resign.
June 10, 1969	COMMONS
In his first budget speech the present Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Sharp) said:
If we do not by one means or another succeed in moderating the increase in aggregate expenditures this year, the most immediate penalty we shall suffer is an inflationary increase in prices.
His prediction has come true in this year of 1909. 'inis budget fails to come to grips with the problems. The records of past Liberal governments are proof of the failure of Liberal policy. Like Belshazzar, the last King of Babylon, this government is weighed in the balance and found wanting. Our leader and party have been suggesting for some time consideration of an income policy for Canada, or wage and price guidelines. I was one of those who asked for these measures on May 27, 1966. The government has done nothing about this other than to form another ministry, that of consumer and corporate affairs. But no effective legislation has accompanied this formation to give force and effect to the war on inflation and high prices. And the record of this government indicates that none ever will. The people of Canada have reached the point of painful and dispirited unexpectancy.

subtopic: THE BUDGET
subsubtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in reporting on the nation's business the Financial Post of June 7 had this headline, "Very tough job nicely handled", and proceeded to commend the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) for attacking inflation directly. He was particularly commended for tariff cuts and for deferring depreciation allowances for commercial construction in urban centres. A number of tax experts and economists called these moves "bold, imaginative and highly sophisticated". Of course, the budget also drew unflattering remarks from the opposition and other critics. The criticism is that it does nothing to halt inflation. The Minister of Finance is accused of favouring high interest rates and it is suggested that instead of creating jobs the budget will aggravate the current unemployment problem, and so on.
With regard to the deferred depreciation on buildings for two years for tax purposes, which is to be applied only to centres of 50,000 population or more in the provinces of Ontario, Alberta and British Columbia, because in the other seven provinces unemployment is relatively high or employment growth has been slower than the national average, I should like to make a few observations which relate to my constituency. In a
DEBATES	9969
The Budget-Mr. Badanai country so vast and comparatively sparsely populated the problem of regional disparity is a most difficult one. Even in good times, some areas may suffer from high unemployment and undeveloped resources. Therefore, the government has wisely introduced specific incentives intended to stimulate depressed regions and to counteract slow growth.
However, while I am in agreement with the concept of the legislation, I do not share the view that there are no slow growth areas or high unemployment in any of the three affluent provinces named by the minister. There is one portion of the province of Ontario, its northwestern corner, of 200,000 square miles in which the cities of Fort William and Port Arthur are situated as well as a string of towns from White River in the east to the Manitoba boundary in the west, where you will find plenty of unemployment, especially among our Indians-and there are thousands of them. This is one of the slower growing areas of the province. I am speaking about a region in the province of Ontario which by no stretch of the imagination shares the high level of prosperity of the eastern or southern part. This is an area which has the type of problems this legislation is intended to cure.
[DOT] (8:40 p.m.)
At this point I should like to mention that for several years this region of northwestern Ontario has tried to gain recognition as a designated area eligible for industrial development incentives. An example of this attempt is a resolution passed at the 1965 annual convention of the northwestern Ontario associated chambers of commerce, which I wish to read:
Whereas:
1.	The federal government has provided incentives for the development of industrial employment opportunities in designated areas in Canada
2.	The government announced its designated area policy already has resulted in 175 new industries of a capital investment of $418,000,000 providing 4,000 new jobs in 23 of the 35 areas
3.	No part of northwestern Ontario is included in the incentives program despite acutely fluctuating seasonal employment and relatively low population density
4.	Northwestern Ontario possesses the basic ingredients for greatly accelerated growth despite its underdevelopment and underpopulation.
Therefore be it resolved: That the Northwestern Ontario Associated Chambers of Commerce request the federal government to apply and provide the incentives related to the "designated area" program to the northwestern Ontario districts of Thunder Bay, Rainy River and Kenora.
June 10, 1969

The Budget-Mr. Badanai On May 5, 1966, a delegation from Northwestern Ontario met with the minister of industry, the minister of finance and the minister of resources and energy. Included in that delegation was our present Minister without Portfolio (Mr. Andras) from Port Arthur and myself. This delegation, representing all facets of public and business life in the region, was accorded an excellent hearing by the ministers. It was pointed out that under the criteria, now being discarded in favour of the new proposed legislation introduced by the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion (Mr. Marchand) a few days ago, our region did not qualify. We recognized the overall objective of stimulating the economy of less affluent sectors of our country through greater industrialization, and the remarkable results achieved under area development legislation in capital investments and employment of many thousands of Canadians in such regions, but, all our arguments were in vain, we simply could not qualify.
A quotation from the delegation's brief reads as follows:
Our hands, in short, are tied securely by our "off limits" status while tax revenues originating in northwestern Ontario help to subsidize this and other industrial enterprises established elsewhere. We pay for a fare on the Good Ship Area Incentive but we can't get aboard. Rather, we are being swamped by the waves.
Here we are, fewer than one quarter of a million people, occupying more than one-half of the land and matter mass of Ontario, an area as large as Manitoba or Saskatchewan. Our population is scarcely 2.5 per cent of the provincial total, less than one per cent of the population of Canada. On our country's 102 birthday, this is hardly a remarkable record of growth for a region as richly endowed as ours. And in the midst of accelerated activity across Canada, in which our area shares, our assessed population is about stationary.
This is not to deny the recent surge of expansion embracing primarily greater development and processing of our forest and mineral resources plus secondary industry to serve this growing complex. Indeed, manufacturing enterprises are proving beyond question that, despite handicaps of a small and scattered regional population, long distances from concentrated markets and transportation costs, production of goods can be carried on successfully in northwestern Ontario.
The brief then continues:
Nevertheless, while we develop our natural resources we continue to lose the most precious resource we possess-our educated youth. They leave our region simply because of insufficient career opportunities. Some leave our country altogether, a national as well as a regional loss.
"One of the reasons for our low rate of unemployment" states . the Fort William Times-Journal in its lead editorial of May 22, "is the fact that 
lack of diversified industries has prompted the exodus of large numbers of young people from the area to find work opportunities in other centres of Canada and the United States. It is a matter of record that in recent years the total labour force locally has lagged, while the labour force throughout the province of Ontario has risen appreciably."
Adds the Port Arthur News-Chronicle in its leading editorial of May 2: "The fact that unemployment for northwestern Ontario as a whole is not high enough to qualify for designation is misleading. One of the reasons for this is that when our young people get their education and grow up they have in the past been forced to move elsewhere to find opportunities. The fact that there are enough people from here in Toronto to form a lively and progressive Lakehead Club of 1,000 members is ample proof of this fact."
On behalf of northwestern Ontario, I ask the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) to forgo the deferment of depreciation and capital cost allowances on commercial buildings in the cities and towns of northwestern Ontario as an aid to construction in this particular portion of Ontario which is still a slow growth area, and which should be considered in the same category as the adjacent province of Manitoba. Had it not been for an Ontario premier of long ago, this region would have formed part of the province of Manitoba. Had that happened, I am among those who believe that the area would have attained a status of far greater importance.
I also wish to raise another matter of concern to the economy of my constituency, and of many others. I refer to the constant cry we hear from the N.D.P. against foreign investment in Canada. We are indeed fortunate in having a finance minister who, like his immediate predecessor, believes that an attempt to restrict foreign investment in Canada is not in Canada's best interest. The members of that party tell us our economy is in great danger of being taken over by what they like to call continentalism, and that we are gradually being absorbed into the industrial structure of the United States without having any say in the matter. Of course there is a great deal of U.S. investment in Canada, but we often forget that while Canada is one of the wealthiest countries of the world it is still a developing country. It is still one of the vastest and emptiest lands in the world. We need more people and more capital to achieve a measure of independence which those opposed to foreign investments claim we can have by shutting out foreign capital.
[DOT] (8:50 p.m.)
Had foreign capital not been available to bring into production the Steep Rock iron mines in northwestern Ontario, the iron ore
June 10. 1969	COMMONS
which recently has been mined would still be at the bottom of the lake. The several thousand workers would, in all probability, be numbered among the unemployed. Then, there is the dollar exchange factor, which has earned millions of dollars for Canada, resulting from this enterprise as well as others such as the pulp and paper industry upon which many of my constituents depend. I could mention many other industries that have brought benefits to Canada as a result of foreign investment.
It is always easier to blame someone else than it is to adopt the sort of policies that would really give greater economic independence to Canadians. Perhaps, we have not yet fully exploited all the possibilities of encouraging a greater flow of domestic savings into the channels of Canadian industrial investment. Unfortunately, Canada has a long way to go before Canadians can invest in sufficient amounts to develop our country's potential. Until that time, foreign investments will be urgently needed to bring to this country the development that Canadians are not willing to bring to it.
It should be obvious to all that foreign capital is needed badly if Canada is to keep financially healthy and growing. More capital means more jobs and more jobs mean prosperity for all. I honestly believe that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) introduced a good budget, tailored to fit the times, with no new personal income or corporation taxes. It will produce relief for consumers through the lowering of tariffs and the duty free concessions to Canadian tourists.
I congratulate the minister for winning more praise than criticism, and I am quite happy to support his worthy effort in giving Canada one of the best budgets to which it has been my privilege to listen since my election to the House of Commons in 1958. If I may, however, I should like to advance a suggestion that if it were possible to implement an exemption for income tax purposes of the municipal tax on a house, an amount which could be fixed, this measure would undoubtedly prove of great assistance to people in the lower income bracket. I venture to say that the revenue lost by this kind of tax concession would in the long run, prove beneficial to all concerned.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure to have an opportunity to say a few words in the budget debate. Unlike the last speaker who, I believe, is the hon. member for Fort William
DEBATES	9971
The Budget-Mr. Harding (Mr. Badanai), on the government side, I fail to see how this can be one of the best budgets that has ever been written. If this is the best budget to which the hon. member has listened since 1958, then the others certainly could not have been worth listening to at all. A great deal depends on how these various budgets affect the different groups in our society. I cannot imagine any of the old age pensioners jumping with glee and delight over the budget which was introduced here one week ago. There is no indication in it that the government is going to give an extra five cents to the large group of old age pensioners who desperately need an increase in their pensions. There is no indication in the budget that the veterans are going to receive an increase in their pensions, despite the promises of the government to bring in a white paper and despite the recommendations in the Woods report. These provisions should have been contained in this budget, not in the budget that will come down in the fall or next spring.
As we go on right down the line through the best budget that my friend has ever heard in his life we find an amazing thing, namely that item after item has been missed. We see nothing in it about the government's attack on poverty in a country where between four million and five million Canadians are living in poverty, in the words of the Economic Council of Canada. This is an amazing thing.

I have outlined several of the problems. One of them is the vast pollution which we are experiencing in Canada. There is only one tiny reference to pollution problems in the budget. This is certainly not a budget of which the Liberal government can be proud. There are groups of citizens in Canada who will be badly hurt simply because the members of this house and the government did not deal adequately with the problems which should have been dealt with in 1969 in this budget.
June 10. 1969

The Budget-Mr. Harding
We are debating a subamendment moved by a member of our party, and I should like to speak very briefly on this subamendment. It is suggested that the income tax exemptions for single people be increased to $2,000 and the exemptions for married people be increased to $4,000, a very modest request and one which every member of this house should endorse. Let us look back at the income tax regulations which were set down many years ago. Here we find old age pensioners being taxed on their meagre income, which is not what the government should be doing.
The Carter Commission brought down their report a while ago in which they pointed out very clearly that we have one of the most unjust tax systems in the whole industrialized western world. What do we find in this great budget, the greatest budget that has come out for many years? Do we see any reference to tax reforms? You bet your life we do not. Carter showed us the way to do it. He showed us where money could be obtained by this government if it had the backbone to go after it. The ordinary individual in Canada-and I am talking of people in the low and middle income brackets-is getting sick and tired of having taxes imposed on him while we are letting off scot-free many other people and corporations on which taxes should be levied. If hon. members over there think this is what a budget should be, then that is Liberal thinking and not my thinking.

speechtext:
We are asking that changes take place. We do not want to wait for them until the end of this parliament. Another budget of an interim nature was brought down last fall. At that time, as during the election, we heard the story that the just society was about to emerge. This is what we were told in June of 1968. Let me remind hon. members that a budget reflects the priorities which a government has in mind and the values it places on various sectors of the economy. It should chart the direction in which we are going. It is an amazing thing to me, but I have not seen any indication that we are heading toward that just society about which government supporters talked so glibly. A just society is not one in which one-fifth of the nation is living in poverty or where huge pockets of regional disparity exist about which precious little is being done. A just society does not ignore the pension needs of the groups to which I have referred. These 
are the fields in which we should be taking action. The budget we are now considering will take us into 1970. Almost half the life of this present parliament will have gone by before another budget is brought down. We have lost all this time. To my way of thinking the government has done a mighty poor job to date. I was hopeful that we would see some changes but like many more individuals I am bitterly disappointed.
There is another aspect from which this budget may be viewed. What has this government done about unemployment, which is one of the major issues confronting us as a nation? I am not playing down inflation; we know inflation is a serious problem. What about unemployment? A budget was brought down last fall, supposedly to do the job which this budget sets out to do. It failed miserably. The cost of living took off from last fall right through this spring, rising more rapidly than ever. During the winter, unemployment rose to fantastically high levels-over 10 per cent in the maritimes, over 8 per cent in Quebec, over 6 per cent in my own province of British Columbia and over 5 per cent across Canada.
How does the budget propose to deal with this situation? It is crystal clear that the government does not expect a significant decline in unemployment figures. The estimate is still that between 400,000 and 500,000 people will be out of work. In the report of the Economic Council of Canada some of the top economists in this nation stated that 3 per cent should be the limit as far as unemployment is concerned, yet month after month we have seen the rate running at double that amount. Does the government not accept advice of the people they hire to check into these things?
It is my frank opinion that the government gets into trouble when it strikes out on its own. Time and time again they get off the track. Changes must be made. We have tried the old solutions and they have not worked. It is time the Liberal party and other parties in this nation began to realise they must take more drastic measures if we are to solve the major difficulties facing Canada today.
I should like to return to the subject of pensions for a moment or two. It is a sad commentary on politicians who are sent to Ottawa that they can do so little effectively to assist those who can no longer bargain successfully for themselves. I am referring to senior citizens, retired civil servants, war veterans and those who have retired on pensions-C.N.R. pensioners, for example. We find that the old age security legislation contains a provision to the effect that if the cost
June 10. 1969

of living rises by 2 per cent pensioners will get a 2 per cent increase. If the cost of living index goes up 4 per cent they will still get a 2 per cent increase. In the last couple of years the spending power of pensioners, and indeed, of all of those on fixed incomes, has rapidly been eroded. Yet we have done nothing about it, though we are in a position to do something about it; we could easily make a change in the legislation which would at least result in the annual raise being equal to the rise in the cost of living index.
The estimate for the increase in the coming year contemplates another 4 per cent, which in other terms means a further $1.50 from the monthly cheque received by our senior citizens, the price of one more item in the stores which they will be unable to buy, though this is one of the richest nations in the world. We should be ashamed of ourselves for failing to tackle this need. We can do it. What are hon. members across the way doing about this? You have a majority in this house. You are the people who should be demanding amendments to the act and demanding that something be done.

speechtext:
Thank you, Mr. Speaker. I certainly will address the members through you. Hon. members on the government side should persuade the various cabinet ministers to bring in necessary amendments along the lines I have just indicated.
[DOT] (9:10 p.m.)
Now, I should like to spend a few minutes considering another question which has worried me a great deal since I came to Ottawa. It is the subject of national unity. Some might wonder why national unity should be brought into a speech on the budget. Well, as far as achieving national unity is concerned, I feel more can be done by dealing with the economic problems facing the nation in the various provinces of Canada than by bringing a measures such as the languages bill. Each step is of assistance, of course, but I believe that this budget has failed, and failed miserably, to solve economic problems and thus do a tremendous amount of good in bringing about unity across the nation. After all, people who are happy, have jobs with adequate incomes and are free from poverty are not going to talk about branching off from a central body. As far as governments are concerned, their real aim should be to try to
The Budget-Mr. Peddle achieve national unity in this nation of ours. I suggest we put far more emphasis on this particular aspect of the economy than we have in the past.
Before my time runs out I should like to make some comments about the deferred depreciation mentioned in the budget, and which some of our Liberal friends have told us is going to be good for the economy by bolstering housebuilding in various sections of the nation. I am not too sure that this is true. Having read the budget rather carefully and surveyed the picture across Canada, it appears to me that this deferred depreciation of 5 per cent a year in the long run is not going to mean very much. My reason for saying that is this: The Minister of Finance himself has estimated that there is going to be a Canada wide increase in costs of 4 per cent. By deferring commercial building the builder cannot claim his 5 per cent depreciation. On t'he other hand, his costs are going to go up 4 per cent. Therefore, I cannot for the life of me see that very much building will be deferred in this situation.
Other hon. members have referred to another rather odd aspect of this particular measure, and that is the singling out from the rest of three provinces with cities of over 50,000 population. I am doubtful that the claim made by t'he Minister of Finance of a saving of some $450 million that might hopefully be channelled into housing will be established in the ensuing year.
My time is almost up, but in closing I should like to say there are many major problems facing the nation. For example, there is unemployment, inadequate pensions, poverty, our taxation system, repatriation of the Canadian economy, high interest rates, cost of living and the great agricultural problems faced especially by the farmers in the west. Frankly, I think this budget does not deal adequately with those problems. In my opinion, and I believe in the opinion of most Canadians when they realize what is behind the budget, it will prove disastrous for the year 1969.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in my remarks in this debate I intend to take advantage of the traditional latitude extended by Your Honour both in this and the throne speech debates and will not necessarily confine my remarks to the content of the budget speech delivered on June 3. For the

June 10, 1969
The Budget-Mr. Peddle most part the budget is, to me, a rather technical document, and as one newspaper columnist put it, it gives no cause either for spontaneous dancing in the streets or for mass protest rallies.
I am sure this is particularly true in Newfoundland. I cannot imagine for the life of me the Newfoundland fishermen becoming overly emotional over the fact that a pound of imported chocolate candy will cost three cents less, or that the cost of a pound of fancy imported raisins will drop almost one cent, or that a can of pineapple will cost four fifths of one cent less, or that a dollar's worth of orange juice will cost one and a half cents less. Certainly, I cannot imagine any Newfoundlanders being overjoyed because they are now allowed to bring back a little more duty free goods from their trips abroad. The few Newfoundlanders who do go abroad have, like most other Canadians, always managed to bring back a little more duty free goods t'han they were allowed.
I am also sure that the people I know best-Newfoundlanders-will not be too upset by the measure to defer capital cost allowances on skyscrapers in Ontario, British Columbia and Alberta. What the people of my province, and I presume the people of the other Atlantic provinces want, and what they have looked for in past years' budgets, throne speeches and government pronouncements, are measures to fulfil the big campaign promise made by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) last June. I refer to the big promise that his government would dedicate itself to the furtherance of the just society concept and the diminution and ultimate elimination of regional disparity.
There are those who say that the Prime Minister-indeed, the Prime Minister himself has said this

made almost no promises in the last election. However, Mr. Speaker, if you think about it for a minute you will realize that the references to the just society and to elimination of regional disparities embody every promise for which any sensible Canadian could possibly ask. After all, who in Canada wants more than justice? Who in Canada demands more than economic parity with his fellow Canadians? I say nobody. The Prime Minister did indeed make promises a year ago, very potent political promises. They were promises that embodied in a few words every other promise that was ever made in Canadian political history.

[DOT] (9:20 p.m.)
In his campaign of a year ago I think the Prime Minister capsulized one hundred years of political promises. He crammed one hundred years of frantic and not so frantic vote getting specifics on the part of all political parties into one potent political pill, his "just society and regional disparity pill". And boy, there is no question that this was a vote getter! I agree that the Prime Minister did not promise anything:	I say that what he
promised was everything. The people of Canada have a right to see those promises fulfilled. I call those promises a pill. The people of Canada swallowed that pill, and a whole year is a long time to wait for the slightest sign of benefit from the medication.
We were justified in expecting that this government's legislative program would reflect immediately, from the beginning its professed concern over injustice in our society and economic disparities between our regions. We expected to see real measures introduced, which would at least help us to begin fighting injustice and disparity. Now, let us look at the legislative program of this session which is about to end and let us look at other issues which have been raised in this country by this government. We have that famous bill C-150, if my memory serves me correctly, to amend the Criminal Code. It legalized homosexuality and liberalized the law concerning abortion. I suppose, too, it legalized abortions. Perhaps it is not proper to dwell on the homosexuality bit, but I think the house ought to hear a quip on this subject. Some wag said, "They have legalized it; next they will make it compulsory." And as someone from the N.D.P. added a few moments ago, "Yes, and without a means test."
The government had its priorities mixed up. We had the government reorganization bill. That was a great time consumer. A few departments were reorganized. Primarily, the bill established the department which is to deal with disparities between various economic regions of the country. We have not heard too much from that department. I presume its people are closeted together and will come up with sheaves of maps, plans, studies, task forces and what have you. Then, we had the languages bill which our party in large part supported and which I, too, supported. But I do not regard the languages question as being of top priority. We considered the housing bill which was brought forward much sooner than we had anticipated as a result of the resignation of the minister who, until
June 10, 1969

then, had been responsible for housing. I suppose the government felt impelled to do something pretty quickly. When you come right down to it, there is nothing in the bill for the low income Canadian, and therefore there is nothing in it for any Canadian. I say that for this reason. If you are not a low income Canadian you have no problem with housing. Therefore, there is nothing in this bill for any Canadian since there is nothing in it for any low income Canadian. So, I ask, what was the use of bringing it forward?
The problem, as I see it, is very simple. You have a young, married man earning $3,000 or $4,000 a year, and he has to pay rent of $125 or $150 a month. Half his salary goes towards maintaining a roof over his head.

speechtext:
This is the problem. I wish the government would stop playing footsie with it and enter fields of endeavour which would help our people. The government is in the transportation business. It is in the hotel business. It flies aeroplanes and runs trains. I say to the government, stop playing footsie and, if necessary, get into the house building business. If that means depriving some of our big people in the building industry of a fat profit, that is their tough luck. After all, the government deprives the people in the hotel or transportation businesses of some of their profits.
During the past nine months the government has acted in some fields without being authorized to do so by legislation. For instance, the recognition of Red China has been under discussion. Why the government is doing this I do not know, but there it is. We have the question of the cutting back of our NATO forces. This sort of thing seems to come up at regular intervals. Then, the question has come up of establishing diplomatic relations with the Vatican. As I say, these suggestions seem to come up regularly. It seems to me someone sits up nights dreaming up ways of dividing the Canadian people and of setting us against other countries. Somebody works the night shift, I am sure, dreaming these things up. Where are the government's priorities, I ask? When I look at what has been done I ask myself, has the government done these things to cover up the fact that it has no real policies to put forward?

subtopic: THE BUDGET
subsubtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
At the beginning of the session, if my memory serves me correctly, we had a budget that raised taxes. A few nights ago, near the end of the session, we had a little budget. In the budget speech the minister tried to tell us that there would be no increase in our taxes. That is just a play on words. When you have promised to discontinue a tax and you continue it in force, what are you doing except increasing taxes? We were told that a certain tax would be removed at the end of this year. Then, the minister turned around and kept the 3 per cent surtax in force. Let's not kid one another, Mr. Speaker. That tax will probably remain in force next year because the minister likes its taste.
Then, we have the tax on air travel which has not been pinned down to definite amounts. We do not know how big that tax will be. It will not affect my Newfoundland constituents too much because not too many of them are lucky enough to be able to afford air travel. Nevertheless, because of our geographic position and because some people may wish to visit their friends in Newfoundland, we want to see air fares kept as low as possible for the benefit of those who are lucky enough to have Newfoundland friends to visit.
The minister has budgeted for a $390 million surplus. All this week he has worn a smile on his face, reminding me of the cat that swallowed the canary. He loves the idea of the $390 million surplus. He is going to get a lot of mileage out of it. At one fell swoop he

June 10, 1969
The Budget-Mr. Peddle will wipe out the $125 million Expo deficit. There is no need to carry it for a number of years; after all, we are rich. Let's write it off, the minister thinks. We have hit the jackpot. After all, we have a $390 million surplus coming this year.
But the people in the remoter areas of Newfoundland who ask the government to build a small wharf costing a few thousand dollars so that fishermen will not drown when they come back from fishing trips and who are refused on the grounds that the government has not the money to build the wharf are not so pleased. What must they think when they are turned down with the excuse that there is not enough money to meet their wishes? What do they think of this surplus? I have a filing cabinet full of letters from these people. They are all nice letters and all express grave concern over this lack of funds. None of them mentions anything about the $390 million surplus which is making the minister so happy. All this reminds me of the man earning, say, $3,000, $4,000 or $5,000 a year who buys a $4,000 or $5,000 automobile and who says to his mother, "Mother, let's pay off the car; we can eat next year or the year after." What kind of nonsense is this? We have regional disparity in Newfoundland. It is made in Canada by the government of Canada. I refer to the matter of permanent military installations.
[DOT] (9:30 p.m.)
Before my time expires I wis'h to quote some figures. The total strength, military and civilian, in the provinces is as follows: Newfoundland, 559; Prince Edward Island, 1,674; Nova Scotia, 20,105; New Brunswick, 7,612; Quebec, 15,227; Ontario, 42,071; Manitoba, 8,785; Saskatchewan, 2,214; Alberta, 8,877; British Columbia, 12,782 and the two Territories 270. I support the brief submitted by the Canadian Legion in the past few days. It states that Newfoundland represents 2J per cent of the population of Canada. Bearing in mind the strategic position of Newfoundland, it is only reasonable we should expect 2\ per cent, or something approaching that, of the total military strength which would amount to 3,000 instead of 559. This is regional disparity, Mr. Speaker. As mentioned in the brief submitted by the Canadian Legion to the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Cadieux), it certainly appears to be in contravention of one of the terms of union. The government said it would maintain suitable military installations in that province. In view of the government's avowed intention to do something about the situation, I very humbly sug-

gest that they start at this point. Then, everyone in Newfoundland will appreciate that and what we hope will follow it.

subtopic: THE BUDGET
subsubtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I had only some very brief remarks to make but having heard the hon. members' speeches about the budget brought down by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson), I would like to say that this budget will not help in any way the Canadian population deprived of purchasing power.
On a few occasions, I had an opportunity to tell the house that a large sector of the Canadian population lacks purchasing power.
Some hon. members have recently poked fun at Social Credit and said that it is a dollar-making machine that could only lead to inflation and that offered some danger.
Mr. Speaker, with all due respect, I would call your attention to the fact that a negative and irresponsible stand will not lead to adequate solutions to that problem which is now facing Canadians, that is an economic system based on the population's needs. Neither will we succeed in selling our huge production, so as to be able to produce more and thus reduce unemployment, by taking money from the tax-payers through direct or indirect taxes.
Everything holds together in the economic system and, in my opinion, we are facing a serious problem in Canada. We have to sell our products and increase our productivity while enabling people to meet their needs. We are more and more convinced that this monetary system is inadequate and cannot solve this problem.
As for us we suggest a solution which certainly will not solve all world's problems but which could at least settle some of them and which I think is justified by the existing conditions which we have been experiencing moreover for 100 years now. I think that hon. members-whatever their political opinions are

should at least be honest enough to examine seriously this solution, not with red-or blue-tinted glasses but so as to determine whether it is the whole or partial answer to our economic problem.
Mr. Speaker, the day I am given proof and sufficient explanation that the theory proposed by Major Douglas a number of years ago and now advocated by the Rallie-ment creditiste is not appropriate, that it does not solve the monetary problem while respecting private enterprise and promoting the development of the human being, I will no
June 10, 1969

longer be a Creditiste because I will know that it is not a true solution.
To date, nothing has been proven. We have not been told that it is an inadequate solution and those who do, act in the same way as the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion (Mr. Marchand) who laughs at us, pokes fun at everything, without seriously considering the suggestion.
The Minister of Finance wants us to study his budget seriously. He would like us to examine his recommendations seriously.
The Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Cote) has invited the members of the opposition to study the budget recommendations seriously, but he has neither the courage nor the sincerity to practise what he preaches and to make the necessary mental effort to examine our proposals.
We are ready to study his seriously, to make a clean sweep in order to examine the financial and economic recommendations of the government. We would hope he would have the same intellectual decency to study in return, with the same intellectual honesty, the recommendations that we bring forth.
Until I have proof to the contrary, it will not be said that the Canadian people have everything they need to live well and to grow. It will not be proven by the government that our productivity will increase, our balance of payments improve, that the purchasing power of the population will climb and our debts diminish.
On the contrary, we notice that debts increase, that our balance of payments is increasingly unfavourable, that we belong more and more to the United States, that the economic situation of several social classes is getting worse all the time, that the gap between rich and poor is getting wider, that the poor grow poorer, and there are more and more of them, that the rich are getting wealthier, but in smaller numbers, and that the situation is becoming unbearable for a large part of our people.
To speak about one part of the population, there are now more than 470,000 unemployed in Canada, who have neither a sufficient income nor the opporunity to work and develop their talents to increase the productivity for the benefit of the country. What is the government doing in that connection? Absolutely nothing!
Mr. Speaker, while some people are unemployed, others earn a living painfully, by the sweat of their brow, and do not make enough money to keep their families decently, to enjoy life.
The Budget-Mr. Fortin
Here, I refer to question No. 636 that I put on the order paper on November 1 last and which the government answered.
I asked how many Canadians earn less than $3,000 a year, and the government answered that 2,440,819 Canadians earn less than $3,000 a year. I have already said it in this house and I say it again that they make up 47.9 per cent of all wage earners.
Mr. Speaker, I cannot think that you, I or another member could keep his family, do this work as a member of parliament, and live decently on a yearly income of less than $3,000. This is ridiculous, Mr. Speaker, in a country as rich as ours.
In this line of thought, I also asked how many people earn between $3,000 and $4,000 a year. You will agree that this is not a very interesting or even acceptable income. It is not even a minimum considering the present cost of living. Moreover, the government is not concerned about this- because it is doing nothing to control the increasing cost of living.
There are, as you probably know, 1,034,909 people in Canada making from $3,000 to $4,000 a year. Those are heads of families, wage earners who work, who are not unemployed and who make only from $3,000 to $4,000, which is a wholly inadequate income to meet their needs and live decently. Well, more than 20.3 per cent of the workers fall in that category.
If we consider the number of Canadians who earn less than $4,000 a year, we see the scandal of the present government that does absolutely nothing to help these people. On the contrary, it keeps on taxing them, "crushing" them further, to use a colloquial term. I believe it is the right one because none other fits to describe the situation in which the government is placing us. 68 per cent of the workers earn less than $4,000 a year.
This evening, a member for the island of Montreal-the name of his riding escapes me because we do not see him often; he was taking the floor for the first time, I think- said that the Ralliement creditiste was advocating the Social Credit doctrine and that it made no sense, that its principles defied application, that everything was going well and that the Minister of Finance deserved congratulations. I suggest that such an attitude is not honest. At least, one should be honest enough to study the solution we are proposing, that is to establish a balance between the purchasing power of the consumers and the total production of the country.
9978

June 10, 1969
Division
We are presently experiencing a period of inflation. The Americans and the American banks have announced that they are tightening credit, that they are increasing the interest rate. We, Canadians, with our sheeplike mentality with regard to economic policy, will follow suit, obviously. Who will bear the brunt of such an attitude? The Canadians, again and always.
Mr. Speaker, I am convinced that we should have, in Canada, a policy of economic nationalism at the service of the people, so that money will serve the people and not the reverse.
